articles.title: 'Hijab on their heads, not minds': Owaisi calls Allahabad HC ruling 'attack on Islam'
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi on Tuesday criticised the Allahabad High Court's dismissal of a minor student's petition seeking permissio.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi on Tuesday criticised the Allahabad High Court's dismissal of a minor student's petition seeking permission to wear a hijab with her prescribed school uniform in Prayagraj. Calling the ruling an "attack on Islam", Owaisi questioned the court's authority to determine what is essential to the religion.Addressing the Jalsa-e-Rahmatul-lil-Alameen gathering at the AIMIM headquarters in Darussalam, Hyderabad, Owaisi said the ruling was inconsistent with the constitutional protections of religious freedom and freedom of expression. He also pointed to the ongoing Sabarimala case before the Supreme Court, where a nine-judge bench is examining questions surrounding essential religious practices.The AIMIM chief said, "A judgment came from the Allahabad high court. A girl was wearing a hijab to school, and the Court ruled that one cannot wear a hijab. I disagree with this High Court judgment; I do not concur with it. The Sabarimala case is already before the Supreme Court, where nine judges are deciding what is essential. Today's verdict violates Articles 25 and 19 of the Indian Constitution. Who are you to decide what is essential to Islam? Girls are wearing hijab on their heads, not on their minds. It is an attack on Islam."The remarks came after a division bench of Justices JJ Munir and Indrajit Shukla dismissed the student's petition challenging the school's refusal to allow her to wear a scarf over her uniform.The court observed that the petitioner had not produced religious scriptures or other material establishing that wearing a scarf was an "essential" part of her religion, such that its absence would affect her faith. It also noted that photographs submitted before the court showed other students from the same religious community attending the school without scarves.The bench held that where a dress code is uniform, non-discriminatory, adopted in good faith and intended to maintain discipline and institutional identity, determining the uniform primarily falls within the school's jurisdiction.The court further said that the student's previous practice of wearing a scarf in lower classes without objection did not create a permanent or enforceable right to require the school to alter its uniform policy. It clarified that the school was not curtailing her freedom of faith but was enforcing institutional discipline, with the uniform forming an essential part of that discipline.The student had completed Class 10 at the same school and sought admission to Class 11. She told the court that she had worn a scarf over her school uniform since Class 6 and that the school had never objected to it.However, when she sought admission to Class 11, the school management informed her that wearing a scarf violated its dress code and refused admission on that ground.Get the latest India News and Live updates. There should be an inquiry into the firing of pellets and bullets, and the government must be fully prepared to take accountability for the same," AISA president Neha Bora told PTI."From AISA, we are seeing that this is a matter which still remains unresolved. The government itself had committed to withdrawing the cases, but still this is a major issue where students who protested against the government have cases against them," she added.The CJP announced the fresh protest on Monday, accusing the Centre of backtracking on its promise to withdraw FIRs against student protesters. The earlier agitation was called off on July 25 after then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan stepped down, which had been the protestersâ primary demand.Bora, who was on a 23-day hunger strike in Delhi last month with climate activist Sonam Wangchuk over the NEET paper leak, argued that the protests became necessary because the government had made dialogue with ordinary people difficult.âThe entire point of why students and youth had come out on the streets and why we came out on the streets was that this government has made it impossible for the common people to have a dialogue with them,â she said.Asked about the government's likely response, Bora maintained that a democratic government should engage with people seeking dialogue.âIdeally, the government of a democracy should listen to people who are coming to have a dialogue with it. articles.title: Libyan cleared after Lockerbie bombing trial dies aged 70
articles.summary: A Facebook post by Libyan Airlines announced the death of Al Amin Khalifah Fhimah and expressed the company's condolences to his family.
articles.body:
A Libyan who was cleared after standing trial over the Lockerbie bombing is reported to have died aged 70.

Al Amin Khalifah Fhimah was accused of murdering 270 people in the attack on Pan Am Flight 103 in December 1988.

He was found not guilty but a second Libyan, Abdulbasset Al Megrahi, was convicted of playing a key role in the bombing of the American airliner.

A Facebook post by Libyan Airlines announced his death and expressed the company's condolences to his family.

Fhimah worked for the carrier in Malta before the bombing of Pan Am 103.

The charges against Fhimah and Megrahi were first announced by Scotland and the United States in 1991.

Years of sanctions imposed on Libya by the United Nations led to the two men being handed over to stand trial at a Scottish court sitting in the Netherlands.

In 2001, three judges convicted Megrahi of mass murder and jailed him for life, but found Fhimah not guilty.

Megrahi died from cancer in 2012, after being freed on compassionate grounds by the Scottish government.

Fhimah always denied any involvement and was welcomed home to Libya by the country's late dictator Colonel Muammar Gaddafi.

In 2022, the FBI revealed that he had been implicated in the case again, through an alleged confession made by another Libyan who is facing trial in the United States.

Abu Agila Mohammad Masud Kheir Al-Marimi is said to have told a Libyan police officer that he took part in a plot to bomb the plane along with Fhimah and Megrahi, when all three were members of the Libyan intelligence service.

Al-Marimi has denied making the bomb that brought down the jumbo jet and claims the confession is false and was made under duress.

The contents of Al-Marimi's alleged confession and other new evidence which has emerged from Libya has led to speculation that Fhimah could have faced a second trial over the attack on the airliner.

The indictment against Fhimah announced by the US Government in 1991 is still outstanding.

Under the Double Jeopardy (Scotland) Act 2011 , a suspect can be tried over the same crime a second time, if there is new evidence - which was not available during the original trial - that substantially strengthens the case against them.

The BBC understands Scottish and US prosecutors would have looked at taking fresh action against Fhimah, if Al-Marimi was convicted by the court in Washington.

But pursuing a prosecution in Scotland or the US would have been legally challenging and politically sensitive, given his acquittal by the Scottish court in 2001.

Al Marimi is now due to stand trial in Washington in January, after a federal court judge agreed to postpone the case for a third time.

The delay, requested by the defence, followed the emergence of "newly discovered" evidence on the case.

The postponement was not connected to Fhimah's reported death.

articles.title: Sugar prices: Indiaâs sugar squeeze threatens its biggest season for sweets
articles.summary: Domestic sugar prices have jumped nearly 40%, forcing India to import 1 million tonnes of the sweetener.
articles.body:
India, the world's largest consumer of sugar, is trying to avoid a bittersweet festive season.

Sugar prices have jumped nearly 40% in the past two months, prompting the government to import 1 million tonnes for the first time in nearly a decade.

The move comes as demand surges from August, with festivals such as Ganesh Chaturthi, Dussehra and Diwali leading into the busy wedding season. Food and beverage companies also begin stocking up for one of their busiest sales periods, adding pressure on wholesale prices.

Production is now expected to be 30.6 million tonnes in the current season, which runs from October 2025 to September 2026 - 11% below the government's earlier estimate of 34.3 million tonnes.

The squeeze has sent prices soaring. A kilo of sugar that cost around 40-45 rupees ($0.42-0.47; £0.31-0.35) in May-June was selling for more than 58-60 rupees in several markets in August, although prices have begun to ease slightly.

But how did a country, which is also the world's second-largest sugar producer, end up needing imports?

The government has blamed lower sugarcane production linked to reduced rainfall during El Niño, hoarding and tighter global supplies after adverse weather hit other major producers.

But experts say another key factor was that India overestimated its own production - and allowed sugar to be exported before the extent of the shortfall became clear.

The government initially approved exports of 1.5 million tonnes this season, adding another 500,000 tonnes in February. Nearly 800,000 tonnes had been shipped before exports were halted in May.

"From allowing exports at the start of the season to ending with an import of a million tonnes is a large variation on production estimates - and that's a big surprise," said Vikram Suryavanshi, a senior analyst at PhillipCapital India.

That matters because India has little sugar to spare. It consumed more than 28 million tonnes last season, not far below what it expects to produce this year.

Nearly three million tonnes is also expected to be diverted to ethanol production, leaving little room for any shortfall.

That is where the imports will help provide a buffer, says Atul Chaturvedi, non-executive director of Shree Renuka Sugars, India's largest sugar refiner and a major ethanol producer.

For three months from 1 September, sugar refineries in special economic zones near ports - which normally import raw sugar, refine it and re-export it - will be allowed to sell duty-free sugar in the domestic market.

The last time India imported sugar for domestic consumption was nearly a decade ago, when the country was grappling with drought.

Other measures are also under way. The Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA) has asked mills to begin crushing cane a fortnight earlier than usual to build stocks as the new harvest starts arriving in October.

But that crop, too, faces risks from erratic weather.

Sugarcane is highly water-intensive, and uneven monsoon rains and prolonged dry spells in key growing states such as Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka have affected the crop. Yields are expected to fall, while thinner cane with lower sucrose content means less sugar can be produced.

"Looking at the climate conditions, the next season is also not going to be a bumper crop, although it is too early for actual assessment," Chaturvedi said.

India has frequently restricted agricultural exports when domestic supplies tighten and prices rise. In 2023, for instance, it banned exports of non-basmati white rice for more than a year after crop damage contributed to rising food prices.

But experts say the failure to anticipate the sugar shortfall before allowing exports has raised questions about the government's forecasts.

"This year, the initial projections for sugarcane production did not materialise due to unusual weather in some parts and disease in certain varieties," said Siraj Hussain, a former secretary at the federal agriculture ministry.

The government has not explained why the scale of the shortfall was not identified before exports were halted on 13 May. It has said production fell below estimates because of sugarcane disease and waterlogging caused by excessive rainfall.

The BBC has contacted the agriculture ministry for comment.

Some commentators have also blamed the diversion of sugarcane to ethanol production for the shortage in a deficit year. Even earlier, sugar mills would set aside around 10% of their output for this, helping stabilise prices in times of excess production.

But India making E20, or petrol blended with 20% ethanol, the standard fuel at pumps this year, just as sugar output is low, has added to the challenge, experts say.

The government disputes how much the policy is to blame. It says the share of cane diverted to ethanol has fallen from 12% in 2022-23 to around 9% in 2025-26, and argues that weak production, hoarding and tighter global supplies are behind the sugar price surge.

Some in the industry agree. Deepak Ballani of the Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA), which represents private mills producing nearly half of India's sugar, says stocks and monthly quotas for sugar released into the market are comfortable. He argues speculation and hoarding, rather than a genuine shortage, are driving prices higher.

The government has capped stocks held by traders and wholesalers at 400 tonnes for three months to curb hoarding.

Suryavanshi, however, disagrees. India has used such measures before, he says, yet prices continued to climb after the latest restrictions were announced. To him, that points to a real supply squeeze.

And India's decision to import comes as supplies are tightening globally.

El Niño has affected rainfall in Thailand, while heavy rain has disrupted cane harvesting in Brazil, the world's largest sugar producer, where mills are also diverting more cane to ethanol. Heatwaves have battered Europe's sugar beet crop, with France expecting its worst harvest in four years.

US government forecasters expect global production to fall to 184.9 million tonnes this season, from a record 186.1 million tonnes the year before.

London white sugar futures hit $541 a tonne in mid-August, their highest since April 2025, while New York raw sugar futures jumped 4% on the day India announced its imports.

For India, however, sugar availability could improve next year if high prices prompt mills to divert less cane to ethanol.

"At current sugar prices, it simply doesn't make economic sense for mills to divert cane juice to ethanol, so India's sugar scenario should be quite all right going forward," Chaturvedi said.

But the bigger lesson from this year's squeeze, he added, is clear: it is a "warning that going forward, we need to be a lot more careful in estimating our sugar crop numbers".

articles.title: Fire in Pakistan hospital nursery kills at least 14 newborns, officials say
articles.summary: A fire at a nursery in a major government hospital in Pakistan's capital killed 14 newborns, hospital officials and the government said.
articles.body:
Islamabad — A fire at a nursery in a major government hospital in Pakistan's capital killed 14 newborns, hospital officials and the government said.

The nursery at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences housed 15 newborns when the fire broke out, hospital officials said. At least one baby was rescued.

Rescue officials said the fire began at about 6:45 a.m., apparently after the compressor of an air-conditioning unit exploded inside the nursery, which is part of the hospital's gynecology ward.

Firefighters quickly responded and extinguished the blaze, and rescue teams were carrying out cooling operations at the site, local media reported.

The ward was cordoned off and ambulances were seen outside the hospital building, a witness told the Reuters news service.

A hospital spokesperson didn't immediately respond to calls from The Associated Press seeking comment.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the deaths and ordered an immediate investigation. A statement from his office confirmed that 14 newborns had died.

"A tragedy involving children is an irreparable loss," Sharif said.

"The circumstances that led to the incident should be thoroughly reviewed, those responsible should be identified, and the strictest possible action should be taken," he added, according to French news agency AFP.

articles.title: Bristol Water issues first hosepipe ban in decades
articles.summary: Bristol Water says it must protect the River Severn, with the West Country in drought.
articles.body:
A water company has announced its first hosepipe ban caused by drought in more than 50 years, following the lead of other suppliers across the West.

Bristol Water says its "temporary restriction", will come into force from 00:01 BST on Thursday 27 August, to protect water resources in the River Severn.

Wessex Water, Thames Water and South West Water have already introduced bans this summer, with the South West formally declared as being in drought earlier this month.

"Introducing a hosepipe ban is never a decision we take lightly, and we fully appreciate the inconvenience it will cause," said Richard Stanbrook, director for drinking water services at Bristol Water.

Heavy periods study to create world's largest biobank

Why parts of the West look like autumn already

Supercars seized ahead of wedding after M5 incident

This marks the first hosepipe ban in the Bristol Water area caused by drought since 1975, when a dry summer was then followed by 16 months of low rainfall.

However Bristol Water also introduced a short ban in 1990 because of a hole in the bottom of the Gloucester and Sharpness Canal, which then collapsed.

In a statement announcing the latest ban, Bristol Water said although the restriction did not come into force until Thursday, people were being asked to follow the ban immediately.

It includes not using hosepipes for watering gardens, washing cars, patios or boats or filling swimming and paddling pools.

When the weather is as dry as it has been this summer, Bristol Water takes more than half of its supply from river sources, including the Severn via the Gloucester and Sharpness Canal.

However, the Environment Agency and Natural Resources Wales have now applied a drought order to protect the river.

Bristol Water has also pointed to warnings around El Niño, a powerful natural climate phenomenon which pushes up global temperatures and could increase the risks of extreme weather.

Stanbrook said: "After an extended period of exceptionally low rainfall, combined with sustained high demand during the warmer weather, our region's rivers are under significant pressure.

"This is reflected in the Environment Agency's decision to apply for a drought order on the River Severn, where we take a proportion of our water during the summer months.

"The water resources we depend on, particularly the River Severn, support the wildlife, habitats and species that rely on water directly or indirectly, and it's critical we all carefully balance public water use with water needed for our natural environment to thrive.

"We take our responsibility for preserving the water environment very seriously and we know our customers do too. With next year predicted to be the warmest year on record, and with the added pressures from El Niño, we must all think about how we can protect the environment for future years, as well as today."

articles.title: In 1906, Quaker industrialist William Bancroft began buying land outside Wilmington to keep it open for the public; more than a century later, 1,359 acres became the largest unit of First State National Historical Park
articles.summary: US News: In 1906, industrialist William Poole Bancroft began buying land in Delawareâs Brandywine Valley to hold it in reserve for the health and well-being of.
articles.body: In 1906, industrialist William Poole Bancroft began buying land in Delawareâs Brandywine Valley to hold it in reserve for the health and well-being of the public. More than a century later, 1,359 acres of that land became the largest unit of First State National Historical Park.The story of the land, however, began much earlier. National Park service says the Brandywine Valley was originally home to the Lenape people, including the seasonal village of Queonemysing. The village was used for fishing and remained relatively undisturbed while Swedish and Dutch traders focused on the larger waterways in the area.That changed as English colonists, many of them Quakers, began moving further into the interior. Their arrival brought major changes to the valley and affected the Lenape community that had lived there. Over time, European settlement expanded into the area, changing how the land was used and occupied.By the early 18th century, Quaker immigrants had established farms and mills along the creeks. The waterways were important because they provided irrigation for fields, power for mills and routes for transportation. As settlement expanded away from the creek banks, farmers cleared more land and built stone farmhouses.The valley later developed a strong agricultural and industrial character. By the mid-19th century, farmers were cultivating much of the best agricultural land. The area also produced wool, finished cloth, paper and clover seeds. But the water-powered mills that had once played an important role gradually became outdated in the second half of the 19th century.Bancroft begins buying landBy the early 20th century, many of the mills along the Brandywine Creek had stopped operating and fallen into ruin. It was during this period that Bancroft began purchasing property in the valley.Bancroft was an heir to the Bancroft textile mills on the Brandywine. Starting in 1906, he bought land from farmers and small-scale industrialists. His stated purpose was to hold the properties in reserve for the health and well-being of the public.Bancroft eventually acquired more than 1,300 acres. About 1,100 of those acres would later become part of the Brandywine Valley tract of First State National Historical Park.His efforts were not limited to simply buying land. In 1919, he formed the Woodlawn Company. The organisation was later renamed Woodlawn Trustees Inc. Its aims included creating affordable housing and acquiring land for parkland and open space.The land remained privately owned but served as a park for many years. That eventually changed when part of it was transferred to the National Park Service.In 2013, roughly 1,105 acres were donated to the National Park Service. Another 254 acres were donated in 2021. Together, these donations brought the Brandywine Valley unit to 1,359 acres, making it the largest unit of First State National Historical Park.Land becomes national ParkThe land had already been used for recreation before it became part of the National Park Service. In 1959, the Woodlawn Trustees began building bridle paths so their officers and guests could explore more of the area.Some of the paths used existing farm roads, while others were newly created for recreation. By 1968, the paths had been opened to the public. People could use them for hiking, biking and horseback riding.The recreational use of the land has continued under the National Park Service. The Brandywine Valley unit now covers 1,359 acres along the border of Delaware and Pennsylvania.In 2024, the National Park Service completed a Comprehensive Trail Plan for the area. The plan sets out a designated shared-use trail network covering 27.8 miles. The plan includes rerouting, repairing and modifying trails in different parts of the Brandywine Valley unit.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Texas wildfire jumps creeks and rivers as powerful winds drive rapid spread
articles.summary: US News: A fast-moving wildfire in north-central Texas has destroyed a family home and business property, burned buildings at a youth camp and forced evacuatio.
articles.body: A fast-moving wildfire in north-central Texas has destroyed a family home and business property, burned buildings at a youth camp and forced evacuations across sparsely populated ranch country west of Fort Worth, while local ranchers opened barns for animals needing evacuation.The Ross Fire began Monday afternoon and spread across more than 78 square miles (200 sq km) in less than 24 hours, moving through lightly populated areas in two counties. Residents said the blaze crossed creeks and rivers as powerful winds pushed it through ranchland.Firefighters had contained only about 8% of the Ross Fire as of Tuesday evening after high temperatures, dry conditions and gusty winds helped drive its rapid spread, according to the news agency Associated Press.Ranchers open barns for livestockRanchers and a livestock commission made barns available to temporarily hold animals needing evacuation. Emergency centres were opened for residents, while some schools cancelled classes.The blaze also threatened ranch properties around Palo Pinto, where aircraft joined crews on the ground in efforts to protect structures."We've thrown everything at this, and we're still having minimal effect," Fire Chief Danny Watkins said.Family business, century-old home destroyedOutside Graford, the fire hit a business that had been in Katie Rochelle's family for generations.The family's canoe rental operation lost its office and repair shop, while a family home built about a century ago was also destroyed. Some of the company's buses and trailers were also destroyed.Rochelle's husband, a local firefighter, helped protect their home overnight as the fire remained active nearby."I don't know how our house survived," Rochelle said. "Now we're waiting and praying."Buildings destroyed at Worth RanchThe fire also reached Worth Ranch, a youth camp on the southern edge of the affected area, destroying several buildings.Scouting America's Longhorn Council said there were no campers or guests at the property when the flames arrived. All personnel were able to leave safely.Officials in Palo Pinto County had confirmed at least five destroyed structures, although authorities were still assessing the extent of the damage.Federal help mobilised as other Texas fires burnTexas Governor Greg Abbott said resources from the Federal Emergency Management Agency would support firefighting efforts. He also urged residents to avoid activities that could start additional fires during the spell of hot, dry and windy weather.The Ross Fire was not the only blaze demanding attention in Texas. Crews were also responding to four smaller wildfires in surrounding Texas counties.More than 50,000 wildfires recorded across USNational Interagency Fire Center data show that more than 50,000 wildfires have been recorded nationwide this year, the highest number for the same point in the year over the past decade. Twelve new large fires were reported on Sunday alone.In Southern California, areas north of Los Angeles were under a red flag warning through Friday, with forecasters warning that new fires could spread rapidly.In Nevada, authorities sharply reduced evacuation orders around Reno after containment of the Hawk Fire reached 85% by Tuesday evening. The blaze had burned about 23 square miles (60 sq km) and destroyed at least 47 homes.Seven people â three first responders and four civilians â were injured. Fire officials said the Hawk Fire was caused by human activity, though investigators had not determined whether it was deliberately set or accidental.Back in Texas, emergency officials expected the Ross Fire to grow further as temperatures rose.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: South Korea police find four bodies on Jeju island as missing persons scandal deepens
articles.summary: A police sergeant has been arrested following accusations that he lied to victims' families and prematurely closed missing persons cases.
articles.body:
Four missing people have been found dead on South Korean holiday island Jeju, as local police face mounting public criticism for allegedly mishandling missing persons cases.

Reports emerged last week that authorities were launching a belated search for a woman reported missing months ago. This sparked criticism of the police for failing to search for her earlier.

The scandal has since deepened with the arrest of a police sergeant, surnamed Bu, who is accused of lying to victims' families and prematurely closing missing persons cases.

Four officers in the sergeant's chain of command have been put on administrative leave and on Tuesday President Lee Jae Myung ordered a sweeping reform of the police force.

Since Saturday, police have found four bodies on the island, including that of 37-year-old Jang Mi-ran who had gone missing in May.

On Monday, her body was located at a palm tree farm about 500 metres (547 yards) from where she was staying. She was believed to have killed herself.

Bu is suspected to have closed Jang's case prematurely without confirming her whereabouts.

According to local reports, Bu had allegedly told Jang's boyfriend that he had spoken to Jang over the phone and she had told Bu she did not wish to speak to her boyfriend.

Police also found the body of a man in his 60s from Jeju City on Saturday.

The man had gone missing on 28 June. Bu had closed his case and reportedly told the family that the man was found "safe" but "does not wish to disclose his location to the family".

"We believed the police when they said my father was safe and waited, but after 51 days, what returned was his body," the man's son told reporters.

It is not yet clear whether Bu was involved in the missing persons cases for two other bodies that were found in coastal villages in recent days.

Police are now examining all the missing persons reports that Bu had handled, which number nearly 300.

Jeju is one of South Korea's most popular tourist destinations.

The island, known for its rows of palm trees and sparkling waters, received more than 13 million foreign and domestic visitors last year.

While violent crime is rare in South Korea, suicide rates are among the highest in the world.

Some experts have said the low crime rate is part of the reason why missing persons cases are not taken seriously.

"After experiencing on the field that the absolute majority of missing adults are found quickly, [the officers] tend to assume all cases are like that," Lee Yung-hyeock, a professor specialising in police science at Konkuk University, told Yonhap news agency.

While more than 70,000 adults are reported missing in South Korea each year, 99% of them are marked as resolved within a month.

On Tuesday, President Lee said during a Cabinet meeting that "the recent breakdown in police discipline and irresponsibility in public safety matters have become serious problems".

Pointing out that the police are likely to wield the most power out of all the state's institutions, he said "the Korean people are questioning whether [the police] deserve this large power".

South Korea's national police chief was grilled by lawmakers at an emergency National Assembly hearing on Monday, during which he admitted that "there is a fault in the system".

This scandal comes at a politically sensitive time for South Korea's police.

The government had recently passed reform to transfer full investigative power from the prosecutors to the police, a move they said was intended to curtail the prosecutors' influence in politics.

However, the reform has been unpopular among the public, who have for many years accused the police of corruption and incompetence.

With reporting by Hosu Lee and Leehyun Choi in Seoul

articles.title: Islamabad: At least 14 babies die in Pakistan hospital fire
articles.summary: The fire broke out in an air conditioning unit at the mother and child unit in one of Islamabad's main hospitals.
articles.body:
At least 14 newborn babies have died in a fire on a hospital ward in Pakistan's capital Islamabad.

The fire broke out on the third floor of the mother and child unit of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital, one of the main state-run hospitals in the city, on Wednesday morning.

An air conditioning unit caught fire, a spokesman for the hospital told the BBC.

There were 15 babies in the ward when the fire broke out, a hospital spokesman said. One baby was rescued.

The babies in the ward were either in incubators or hooked on oxygen equipment, Pakistan's Health Minister Mustafa Kamal told Geo News. Oxygen is not flammable on its own, but it can accelerate a fire, making materials burn hotter and faster.

Emergency responders rescued at least 19 other people from the hospital, including 10 women, seven children and two men.

The newborn babies who died in the fire have been badly burnt, and will need to be identified in through DNA tests, police said.

Only after the DNA tests can the bodies be returned to their parents.

Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed his "deep sorrow and heartfelt regret" over the hospital fire, and instructed the authorities to "conduct an immediate investigation", according to the statement from his office.

"Such a situation with children is irreparable", the statement said.

Islamabad's District Magistrate has formed a fact-finding committee to investigate the fire which must produce a report "within 24 hours".

Outside the hospital, one man told the BBC his three-day-old baby had died in the fire.

There was a sense of shock among the families who gathered by the entrance, crying by the side of the ward.

Hivsa Walid told the BBC she was inside the hospital when the fire broke out, with her sister-in-law who had given birth in the days before.

She said they were in the nursery opposite the room where the fire started. They heard a shout and initially thought someone had died but then saw the smoke. They grabbed the baby - who is so young she's not yet been named - and ran.

Police have been patrolling the entrance of the hospital, and the glass from shattered windows lay scattered on the pavement mixed with medical masks.

The PIMS is one of the biggest hospitals in Pakistan's capital, with 156 beds in its maternal and child health unit.

Pakistan has dealt with a number of major fires in recent years, often due to poor safety laws and building codes as well as lax enforcement.

In January, a fire ripped through the Gul Plaza shopping centre in Pakistan's largest city of Karachi, killing 67 people.

articles.title: Teenage cyclist dies after hit-and-run collision at Nugentstown, Kells
articles.summary: A teenager has died after a hit-and-run collision in Nugentstown, County Meath in the Republic of Ireland.
articles.body:
A man in his late teens has died after a hit-and-run collision in County Meath in the Republic of Ireland.

Gardaí (Irish police) said the incident involving a van and a bicycle occurred at about 20:05 local time on Tuesday at Nugentstown, Kells.

They said the van failed to remain at the scene, where the cyclist was pronounced dead.

The coroner has been notified and the road remains closed.

Gardaí have appealed for any witnesses to the incident to come forward and have asked anyone with camera footage, including dash cam or mobile phone recordings, to "make this footage available" to them.

articles.title: Instagram head Adam Mosseri admits few teens used âTake a Breakâ feature before default setting; says âMost teens donât want itâ
articles.summary: Tech News News: Instagram head Adam Mosseri has said that only a small percentage of teenagers used Instagram's âTake a Breakâ feature before the company made it a de.
articles.body: Instagram head Adam Mosseri has said that only a small percentage of teenagers used Instagram's âTake a Breakâ feature before the company made it a default setting for young users. The feature, which encourages users to step away from Instagram after spending a set amount of time on the app, became a key point of discussion during an ongoing US trial examining whether Meta designed Instagram and Facebook in ways that could make children addicted to them. âMost teens didn't want it,â Mosseri said. âWe decided to push forward with it anyway.âAdam Mosseri said the feature was used by only a low-single-digit percentage of teenagers before Instagram changed its approach in September 2024, nearly three years after launching it.Instagram's 'Take a Break' feature and teen safety under scrutinyAdam Mosseri, who has led Instagram since 2018, testified in a federal court in Oakland, California, as part of a lawsuit brought by 29 US states against Meta. When an attorney representing Colorado questioned him, Mosseri acknowledged that few teenagers had used the âTake a Breakâ feature before it was turned on by default. However, he rejected claims that Instagram deliberately delayed making the safety feature the default option.When the feature was launched in December 2021, Mosseri had said that early tests showed more than 90% of teenagers who turned it on continued using it. The feature encourages users to close Instagram and take a break after a set period.The case is being closely watched as one of the biggest legal tests of social media's impact on young users.US states accuse Meta of designing addictive platformsFour states â California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey â have accused Meta of designing its platforms in ways that could keep young users engaged and contribute to anxiety, depression and suicide. Meta has denied the allegations and said its research found no clear link between adolescents' social media use and a lack of well-being.All 29 states involved in the lawsuit have also accused Meta of improperly collecting and using the personal data of children under 13. The states could seek nearly $200 billion in civil penalties, according to Reuters.Mosseri also denied allegations that Instagram tried to hide information related to children's safety. âI am not trying to encourage my team to hide anything,â he said. âI want to understand how things work. I can't think of any time that I've encouraged people to bring less information to me.âGet the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Stranded for 11 months, no wages for 5: 7 Indian seafarers repatriated from Abu Dhabi tanker
articles.summary: India News: Seven Indian seafarers allegedly stranded aboard the oil products tanker MV Sea Star 2 at Mina Zayed Port in Abu Dhabi for 11 months have been repatri.
articles.body: Seven Indian seafarers allegedly stranded aboard the oil products tanker MV Sea Star 2 at Mina Zayed Port in Abu Dhabi for 11 months have been repatriated, while efforts are under way to bring home the remaining crew members.In a post on X, the Embassy said it "is closely following up with local authorities on the welfare and early repatriation of Indian seafarers stranded aboard SEA STAR 2. Seven seafarers have already been repatriated, and efforts are underway for the safe and early repatriation of the remaining seafarers."According to FSUI, the remaining seafarers have not received wages for five months. The union also alleged that the vessel's owner deducted visa and travel expenses from earlier payments and that important travel documents remain under the control of port authorities.FSUI had urged the ministry of external affairs, Directorate General of Shipping, Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways and International Transport Workers' Federation to intervene, demanding payment of the outstanding wages and immediate repatriation of the crew. India steps up focus on seafarer safetyThe development comes amid heightened concerns over the safety of Indian seafarers operating in waters affected by the Iran conflict. articles.title: Meet Nimaya Williams, the North Carolina junior who completed free college-planning steps and became one of only two students nationwide to receive a $40,000 BigFuture scholarship
articles.summary: US News: For many high-school students, preparing for life after graduation can feel overwhelming. College applications, career choices, financial planning, an.
articles.body: For many high-school students, preparing for life after graduation can feel overwhelming. College applications, career choices, financial planning, and scholarship searches can all seem like separate challenges, especially for students who are still figuring out what they want their future to look like. For Nimaya Williams, a junior at Westover High School in Fayetteville, North Carolina, taking practical steps toward that future recently brought an unexpected reward: a $40,000 scholarship that could help change the course of her college journey. Williams was selected by College Board's BigFuture as one of only two students nationwide to receive the monthly $40,000 BigFuture Scholarship, according to a July 2026 news release from Cumberland County Schools. She earned the award by completing college and career planning activities through BigFuture, College Board's free online platform.A surprise worth $40,000Williams did not expect her college-planning efforts to result in such a major award. When she received the surprise announcement, the Westover High School junior was overcome with emotion. âIâm about to cry. This is life changing,â Williams said in the Cumberland County Schools release, adding that she felt she was âdestined to do great things.âThe recognition came as Williams worked through the steps offered by BigFuture, a platform designed to help students prepare for life after high school. Rather than requiring students to win an academic competition or submit a traditional scholarship essay, the programme rewards eligible students for taking proactive steps toward college and career planning. For Williams, those actions ultimately led to one of the programme's largest monthly awards.Turning planning into opportunityThe BigFuture Scholarship is connected to activities that encourage students to think seriously about their futures. BigFuture helps students explore potential careers, prepare for college, and find ways to finance higher education. Williams' story highlights that college preparation does not necessarily begin with filling out an application. It can start much earlier, with students exploring career interests, learning about colleges, and thinking about how they will finance their education.That approach can be particularly important for high-school students who may not yet have a detailed plan for what comes after graduation. Taking smaller steps can help make a complicated process more manageable. Williams' scholarship also demonstrates how planning can sometimes open unexpected doors for students.A major relief for her familyThe $40,000 award could have an impact beyond Williams herself. Her mother, Shantay Dupree, said the scholarship would create more opportunities for her daughter while easing some of the financial pressure surrounding college. Dupree said Williams has many strengths and described the scholarship as an important step toward her future. She also acknowledged that paying for college can be difficult for families when money is tight.For families facing the rising cost of higher education, a scholarship of this size can make a meaningful difference. It can reduce the amount the student and family need to cover through savings, loans, or other financial assistance. The award therefore represents more than a moment of recognition for Williams. It could provide additional flexibility as she prepares for college.No essay or GPA requirementOne notable aspect of the BigFuture Scholarship programme is that students do not have to meet traditional academic requirements to be eligible. According to Cumberland County Schools, the programme does not require an essay, test score, GPA, or family-income qualification.The programme awards both $500 and $40,000 scholarships to eligible students attending two- or four-year colleges. The programme awards two $40,000 scholarships and hundreds of $500 scholarships each month. Since the programme began in 2019, BigFuture has awarded more than $25 million in scholarships to more than 30,000 students who took proactive steps toward their futures, according to the school district's announcement. That makes Williams' achievement part of a broader effort to encourage students to begin preparing for college and careers before graduation.A step toward her futureWilliams' story shows that preparing for college does not always have to mean accomplishing something extraordinary overnight. Sometimes, it begins with completing one planning activity, exploring a career, or learning more about financing education. Her decision to take those steps through BigFuture ultimately brought an unexpected $40,000 opportunity.For Williams and her family, the scholarship arrives at an important point in her high-school journey. With another year before graduation, she now has additional financial support as she considers what comes next. What started as a practical effort to plan for college has turned into a significant milestone, one that could help Williams move toward the future she already believes she is destined to achieve.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Kriti Sanon Rakhi ad: Giva jewellery drops Bollywood actor's Indian festival ad over outfit
articles.summary: Kriti Sanon has defended the ad in which she was seen celebrating the upcoming Hindu festival of Rakhi.
articles.body:
An Indian jewellery brand has removed their new advertisement for the upcoming festival of Rakshabandhan, also known as Rakhi, after backlash over the outfit worn by the female lead.

The ad featured popular Bollywood actor Kriti Sanon celebrating the Hindu festival in which sisters tie a thread called Rakhi over their brothers' wrists.

Sanon, who is seen in a cropped top, skirt and a cape, addressed her critics on Tuesday night saying "culture and traditions are in a woman's heart, not in her neckline!"

The row started earlier on Tuesday after actor and BJP MP Kangana Ranaut called the ad "intentionally creepy" and asked why someone would tie a Rakhi dressed in a bikini.

In her comments posted on social media, Ranaut did not name Sanon, but appeared to be referring to the actor.

"It is a wonderful time to be a woman, our closets are full of variety of clothes... From all the options that are available to us today why would you tie your brother a Rakhi in your bikini/under garments? Where are all your styling options? The advert looks intentionally creepy," she wrote.

Her remarks quickly drew attention online, with some users echoing her criticism of Sanon's outfit saying it was too revealing and inappropriate for a traditional festival.

One commentator described her top as a bralette, saying there was a "clear line between modern styling and basic sensitivity towards Hindu festivals".

"Pairing a bralette outfit with a sacred occasion like Rakshabandhan felt completely out of touch and unnecessary," she posted on X.

Others objected to a scene in the advertisement in which the actor also ties a rakhi on her pet dog.

But Sanon also received support, including from Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, who defended her, saying what a woman chose to wear was her own decision. Others accused Ranaut of moral policing.

Some also pointed out that though Ranaut has been more conservative in her clothing in recent years after becoming a politician, she herself often wore short dresses and Western outfits in her films and at social gatherings.

Sanon responded to the critics in an Instagram story, calling out the mindset that questioned women for their sartorial choices. Like Ranaut, she did not name anyone directly.

"The essence of festivals is not in the clothes you wear, it is in the emotions and meaning you hold for the traditions... When will we stop telling women what to wear?? Ethnic fashion has evolved over the years, but still a woman's respect for her culture is measured with just her clothes!! Culture & Traditions are in her heart, not in her neckline!"

Sanon also addressed the issue of tying Rakhi to her pet, saying though the festival traditionally celebrates the bond between a brother and sister, its spirit was about protecting loved ones - which, for her, included her sister and her pet.

Despite her spirited defence, jewellery company Giva announced on Wednesday it was pulling the ad.

"We have the highest regard and deep respect for Indian culture, traditions and festivals. As a brand, we have always believed in celebrating these joyous moments with the entire family and this time we wanted to extend the love and celebration to our pets," Giva said in a statement , external on Instagram.

The Indian woman who stood up to moral policing - and won a pageant

"If our recent advertisement has inadvertently hurt the sentiments of some segments of society, that was not our intent at all. Out of respect, we have withdrawn the advertisement from all media," it added.

Giva is not the first Indian brand to withdraw an ad after criticism on social media. In 2020, popular jewellery brand Tanishq withdrew an advertisement featuring an interfaith couple after it faced right-wing backlash online.

Debates over what women should - and shouldn't - wear have also repeatedly sparked controversy in India.

Last year, a beauty pageant contestant was commended for standing up to a group of men who tried to bully her and other contestants over the skirts and western dresses they were wearing.

In 2021, there was outrage after a 19-year-old student, who turned up in shorts to take an exam, was forced to wrap a curtain around her legs after the teacher objected to her clothes.

In the same year, thousands of women - and some men - shared photos of themselves wearing ripped jeans after the chief minister of the northern state of Uttarakhand criticised a woman for wearing them.

articles.title: The RSF’s defeat will not end Sudan’s war but merely fragment it
articles.summary: Sudanese army’s battlefield gains rely on an armed coalition it may struggle to control once the common enemy is gone.
articles.body:
Sudan’s army has had a good summer. Last month, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) recaptured several towns along the strategic Export Road, known locally as Sadirat, which connects the central Nile valley to the country’s west, and pushed the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) into a defensive crouch across much of the centre of the country.

On the back of these gains, SAF leaders are now speaking more confidently of defeating the RSF entirely, rather than merely containing it.

But look east, to Sudan’s Blue Nile state, and the picture inverts. In mid-August, the RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (led by Abdulaziz al-Hilu), retook Kurmuk and seized Geisan within days, in attacks that Sudanese military sources said were launched from across the border in Ethiopia. Drone attacks on multiple army-controlled cities this month also showed that the RSF’s reach extends well beyond Darfur, its main territorial stronghold.

The lesson of the summer, then, is not that the SAF is on the verge of decisive victory. It is that military victory and political resolution are becoming two very different things. Even a full RSF defeat may not end Sudan’s war so much as fracture it into several smaller conflicts.

A look at the coalitions doing the fighting helps explain why. The anti-RSF coalition is coordinated and led by the SAF, but the army also relies on allied armed movements, including Darfuri factions that signed the 2020 Juba Peace Agreement (JPA). These include Finance Minister Gibril Ibrahim’s Justice and Equality Movement (JEM) and the Sudan Liberation Movement, led by Darfur Governor Minni Minnawi. The JPA required their forces to be integrated into Sudan’s military and security services, but they have been reluctant to give up the military autonomy that underpins their political leverage.

Yasser al-Atta, then assistant commander-in-chief and now army chief of staff, announced in March that the army would activate mechanisms to organise and integrate allied irregular groups into the formal military and security services, but little has happened since.

Al-Atta wasn’t even the first to promise to address the problems of the proliferation of weapons and armed groups. Two years earlier, deputy commander-in-chief Shams al-Din Kabbashi told a graduation ceremony for Minni Minnawi’s Sudan Liberation Movement fighters that the army had “begun enacting a law and structures to control the many popular resistance groups”, warning that the array of semi-autonomous militias, tribal coalitions and volunteers backing the SAF’s war efforts, the “popular resistance” as it is called, would “become the next danger if we continue this way”.

More than two years on from Kabbashi’s speech, the underlying problem remains largely unresolved.

Then there is the RSF’s own coalition, which is actively fragmenting. A string of senior figures, al-Nour al-Qubba, al-Savanna, and more recently, the RSF-appointed governor for the Kordofan region, Hamad Khalifa, have defected, amid reports of Saudi financial inducements as well as tribal grievances.

When al-Nour al-Qubba left, he took dozens of combat vehicles and a large contingent of fighters with him. Given that the RSF is a franchise more than a unified fighting force, these defections should worry the SAF as much as they comfort it: defectors often arrive as intact forces loyal to their commanders, not soldiers used to reporting to a chain of command. In a way, the SAF inherits the RSF’s structural weakness with each defection.

Another example is Abu Aqla Keikel, an SAF-trained officer who initially fought on the army’s side after the war erupted in 2023, before defecting to the RSF later that year and then back to the SAF in October 2024. His Sudan Shield Forces remain, in practice, more under his own command than the army’s, even as he appears alongside SAF leadership and Darfuri commanders at recent battlefield-victory photo ops.

Many commanders inside the anti-RSF camp maintain a fairly wide margin of operational independence and consequently their own political calculations. This will become far more apparent once the war ends and there is no longer a common enemy to paper over the differences.

Sudan’s Islamists, meanwhile, occupy a strange position. Brigades like al-Baraa ibn Malik, affiliated with Sudan’s Islamic Movement, which underpinned Omar al-Bashir’s former ruling National Congress Party (NCP), supplied thousands of fighters and were instrumental in retaking Khartoum from the RSF. The United States has sanctioned al-Baraa ibn Malik, while the European Union has sanctioned its leader, al-Misbah Abu Zaid. Amid this international pressure and SAF battlefield gains, some Islamist fighters and leaders have begun pulling back, in what one Sudan Tribune report described as a “tactical withdrawal”. Al-Misbah recently posted that “we have returned to our civilian lives”.

But retreating from the battlefield is not the same as retreating from politics. Ahmed Haroun, chairman of the former ruling NCP, told Reuters news agency last year that the Islamic Movement could support an extended period of army rule, with an eye towards returning to government through “the ballot box”, as Haroun put it.

Indeed, another potential flashpoint for the SAF is that the war has given fighters in Islamist brigades like al-Baraa ibn Malik years of battlefield experience. There is little reason to think fighters who helped recapture the capital will disarm and disband the moment the war is over, at least not without a political settlement that creates a path for demobilisation.

This is the context in which SAF chief and de facto president General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan’s recently announced national dialogue should be read, less as a comprehensive resolution to the country’s militia problem than as a political process that could convert the army’s wartime alliances into post-war influence.

Burhan has explicitly ruled out the return of RSF leaders to power, promising there would be no “ incomplete peace ” that allowed Hemedti or other RSF leaders back into government. Given the RSF’s abysmal human rights record during the war, the exclusion is defensible, but the broader armed-group problem remains unresolved: namely, how the RSF’s remaining forces would actually be dismantled or integrated, particularly in Darfur, and how the SAF’s own allied militias would be brought under a single chain of command once the shooting slows down.

Another structural problem that is older than this war reinforces why claims of total victory remain elusive. The Sudanese army has long struggled to project sustained power across the country’s peripheries. Under Omar al-Bashir, the government relied on Janjaweed militias to help the army fight the rebellion in Darfur. In 2013, many Janjaweed fighters were brought into the newly created RSF.

There is little reason to think a hollowed-out, cash-poor SAF, dependent on volunteer recruits, Islamist militias and Juba Peace Agreement signatory forces, can now succeed where the pre-war state repeatedly struggled: in Darfur, a region roughly the size of France, where the RSF continues to use cross-border supply routes.

Even if the RSF is somehow eventually broken, its weapons and its fighters will not simply disappear. They will pass to whichever political entrepreneur is best positioned to pick them up. Meanwhile, in Khartoum, the questions of the day after will pry open conflicts that the war has, for now, kept closed.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: In the 1940s, a New York handyman began expanding a cabin with railroad ties and cast-off objects; it grew into a seven-storey labyrinth with around 35 caverns and alcoves
articles.summary: US News: Explore the extraordinary story of Clarence Schmidt's House of Mirrors, a unique seven-storey architectural marvel built from discarded materials in Woodstock, NY. Learn about its origins, growth, and artistic significance.
articles.body: Clarence Schmidt did not set out to build one of Americaâs strangest houses. What began as a modest cabin on a wooded mountainside in Woodstock, New York, became an enormous handmade environment of rooms, walkways, balconies, gardens, grottoes and shrines. Built without a conventional architectural plan, the structure expanded as Schmidt found new materials, developed new ideas and reshaped the landscape around him. At its fullest form, the House of Mirrors extended nearly seven storeys down the mountainside and contained roughly 35 caverns and alcoves.According to Philadelphiaâs Magic Gardens, Clarence Schmidt (1897â1978) moved to Woodstock in the 1940s and, having trained as a mason and plasterer, found work as a handyman. His first home, Journeyâs End, began as a simple log cabin made from railroad ties. Schmidt tarred the exterior and covered it with cracked glass, transforming the modest cabin into an unusual reflective structure. The cabin became the starting point for a much larger environment, which Schmidt expanded and altered as he developed the mountainside site.A cabin that kept growingBy the 1940s, Schmidt was reshaping the mountainside around his home. He cleared sections of the steep slope and built retaining walls from locally quarried bluestone, creating terraces that allowed him to work with the terrain. He later built another cabin around a large tree, which became his living quarters and was eventually known as the Inner Sanctum. From there, the project expanded through successive additions rather than according to a fixed architectural plan. Schmidt added rooms, corridors, elevated sections and other structures, connecting them with stairs, galleries, wooden walkways and balconies. The House of Mirrors developed as an interconnected environment that followed the contours of the mountainside rather than the conventions of a traditional house.The landscape continued to shape Schmidtâs approach. Instead of flattening the site to create a conventional building plot, he worked around the existing contours, fitting new sections around structures that were already in place. Walls followed the terrain and terraces stepped across the hillside, while each addition became part of a larger, increasingly complex environment. According to Ricco/Maresca, the House of Mirrors evolved organically as Schmidt continually added and altered elements in response to the landscape. Its windows and reflective surfaces became distinctive features, while the growing structure incorporated roughly 35 alcoves and caverns connected by corridors, galleries and staircases.Where discarded objects became part of the architectureSchmidtâs materials were as unconventional as his approach to construction. Alongside wood and stone, he incorporated mirrors, pieces of glass and objects that had little connection to traditional house building. Discarded items collected from around the area were given new roles within the structure, becoming part of its walls, surfaces and decorative elements. Woodstock Arts notes that Schmidt incorporated a striking assortment of found objects into the House of Mirrors, including car bumpers, wheels, bicycles, lawnmowers, guitars, saw blades, beer cans and doll parts.The result was an immersive environment in which ordinary building materials existed alongside reflections and found objects. Visitors could move through wooden passages and interconnected spaces containing glass, plants and handmade decorations. Some areas resembled grottoes, shrines or outdoor enclosures rather than conventional rooms. This approach placed Schmidt within the tradition of self-taught artists who created what are now known as art environments, works that blurred the boundaries between sculpture, architecture, gardening and everyday life. Rather than simply decorating a house, Schmidt transformed the structure itself into an evolving artwork.A fragile masterpiece that disappearedAs the structure became more elaborate, it also became increasingly fragile. Schmidt relied on improvised construction techniques and unconventional materials, including roofing tar, which he used to attach objects and coverings to parts of the structure. In January 1968, the House of Mirrors was destroyed by fire, leaving photographs and written accounts as the main records of the environment he had created. However, Schmidt continued building after the loss. He began another structure, known as Mark II, but it too was destroyed by fire in 1971. His work nevertheless left a lasting impression on other artists, including Philadelphia artist Isaiah Zagar. As a student at Pratt Institute, Zagar visited Woodstock and encountered Schmidtâs environment, an experience that influenced his ideas about art and later informed the development of Philadelphiaâs Magic Gardens.Schmidt died in 1978, while the House of Mirrors had already disappeared from the mountainside. Its legacy endured as an important example of an art environment created outside conventional architectural and artistic systems. Its significance lay not only in its extraordinary appearance, but also in the way Schmidt transformed an ordinary cabin into an evolving handmade world. He used materials around him, worked with the landscape and continued adding to the structure until architecture, sculpture and the mountainside became closely intertwined.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 47-year-old California pastor makes college football roster 30 years after an injury ended his career, inspired by a video of a 60-year-old player
articles.summary: US News: A 47-year-old California pastor has returned to college football nearly three decades after an injury ended his playing career, after his son showed h.
articles.body: A 47-year-old California pastor has returned to college football nearly three decades after an injury ended his playing career, after his son showed him a video of a 60-year-old man playing the sport. Justin Buzzard, a pastor, husband and father of three, has made the San José City College Jaguars roster as a defensive end after spending years away from competitive football. Buzzard played football in high school and continued into college before injuries forced him to stop in the 1990s. Decades later, a video showing an older man playing football prompted his son to ask whether his father could make a similar comeback. Buzzard took the challenge seriously, began training again and eventually contacted San José City College. After working through practices and conditioning with players far younger than him, he earned a place on the roster and is now preparing for the 2026 season.How a 47-year-old California pastor returned to college footballBuzzard's return began with a challenge from his son rather than a long-planned attempt to revive his football career. According to Buzzard's account to NBC Bay Area, his son showed him a social-media video featuring a man in his 60s playing football and questioned why his father could not get back on the field. Buzzard initially thought the suggestion was unrealistic, but the idea stayed with him. He eventually contacted San José City College and asked about the possibility of joining the football programme. That conversation led to an opportunity to train with the team, where Buzzard had to demonstrate that he could handle the physical demands of college football. He began conditioning and participating in practices during the summer, working towards the same goal as much younger players. The decision represented a return to a sport he had left behind almost 30 years earlier after injuries ended his original playing career.An injury ended his first football career in the 1990sBuzzard already had years of football experience before his unusual comeback. He played four years of high-school football and then spent one year playing at college level, but injuries eventually forced him away from the sport. Nearly three decades later, he has returned to the field as a defensive end for the San José City College Jaguars. His age makes the comeback unusual, but his previous experience also means he is not learning football from scratch. The challenge has instead been rebuilding the physical conditioning required to play a demanding contact sport after years away. Buzzard has spoken about wanting to remain healthy while competing alongside players who are young enough to be his children. His return is therefore not simply a symbolic appearance. He has gone through the process of training, practising and earning a place on the roster.He made the roster alongside much younger playersBuzzard's teammates are predominantly traditional college-age athletes, creating an enormous age gap between him and many of the people sharing the field. Reports say some of his teammates are around the age of his oldest son, yet Buzzard has said the players have welcomed him rather than treating him as an outsider. His teammates have reportedly given him the nickname "OG", reflecting his status as the oldest player in the group. San José City College coach Jim Winkler told ChurchLeaders that Buzzard was expected to follow the same standards and rules as everyone else on the team. Buzzard has also made clear that he does not want younger players to go easy on him because of his age. His goal is to compete on the field rather than simply serve as an inspirational presence on the sidelines. The fact that he earned a roster place after going through the team's preparation process makes the comeback more significant than simply showing up for a practice.His family had concerns about the physical risksBuzzard's decision to return to contact football also required support from his family. He has been married for more than two decades and has three sons, and his wife initially had reservations about him actually playing in games. Buzzard told Fox News that she was happy for him to make the team but did not initially want him to take part in games because of the potential for injury. Her position later softened, and reports say she now has his games on her calendar and plans to support him. Buzzard has also emphasised the importance of staying healthy as he prepares for the season. The concern is understandable given that injuries were what ended his original football career. His comeback therefore involves a genuine physical risk, particularly because he is returning to a contact sport after a prolonged absence. Nevertheless, Buzzard has continued with the programme and has made clear that he wants to see how far he can take the opportunity.Football is now part of his life alongside his ministryBuzzard's return to the field is taking place alongside his work as a pastor. He is the founder and lead pastor of Garden City Church in the South Bay and has spent years speaking about personal growth, fatherhood, relationships and taking meaningful risks. His football comeback has naturally become connected to that message. Buzzard has described his philosophy with the phrase "risk or rust", arguing that people should continue challenging themselves rather than allowing fear or comfort to prevent them from pursuing meaningful goals. The football experiment gives him a personal example of that philosophy. He is attempting something physically demanding that he had not done for decades while continuing his responsibilities as a pastor, husband and father. His return has therefore become more than a sports story for him. It is also an example of the idea that people can revisit ambitions they once considered finished.His goal is to compete during the 2026 seasonMaking the roster was only the first milestone in Buzzard's comeback. He wants to remain healthy, participate in the season and have an opportunity to contribute on the field. He wears No. 48, a reference to the age he will turn in September. His preparation has involved training alongside much younger athletes, and he has said that he does not expect special treatment because of his age. The San José City College Jaguars are preparing for the 2026 season, giving Buzzard the opportunity to turn an unusual comeback story into an actual competitive season. How much playing time he receives remains to be seen, and simply making the roster does not guarantee that he will appear regularly in games. For now, however, he has achieved the part that once seemed almost impossible. A career that ended with injury in the 1990s has been revived nearly three decades later, after a conversation with his son gave him the push to try again.A decades-old football dream has a second chanceBuzzard's story stands out because the comeback was not the result of a professional opportunity or a carefully planned athletic campaign. It began with his son showing him a video of an older football player and asking a simple question. Buzzard could have dismissed the idea because of his age, his previous injuries or the decades that had passed since he last played. Instead, he decided to find out whether a return was possible. He trained, approached a college programme and eventually earned his place alongside players decades younger than him. Whether he becomes a regular contributor during the season remains uncertain, but the achievement has already given him the chance to finish a chapter that was abruptly ended by injury. For Buzzard, the return to football is also an opportunity to demonstrate the message he has encouraged others to follow: an old setback does not necessarily have to determine what comes next.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1917, the Crane family bought the first piece of Choate Island; decades later, the island entered the Crane Wildlife Refuge under the Trustees in 1974
articles.summary: US News: Explore the fascinating transformation of Choate Island from a thriving agricultural landscape to a protected wildlife refuge. Discover its historical significance, diverse ecosystems, and the legacy of the Crane family.
articles.body: For centuries, the island supported Indigenous communities, farms, livestock and family homes before becoming a wildlife refuge on the Massachusetts coast. Choate Island, once known as Hog Island, is now the largest island in the Crane Wildlife Refuge, where salt marsh, grassland and forest frame historic buildings that date back more than two centuries. Its transformation was gradual, beginning with the Crane family's early-20th-century land purchases and ending with Miné Crane's 1974 gift to The Trustees of Reservations.According to The Trustees of Reservations, Choate Island is the largest island in the Crane Wildlife Refuge, covering 135 acres within the refuge’s 697-acre network of coastal islands and marshes in the Essex River Estuary. More than 200 bird species have been recorded across the refuge, while Choate Island provides habitat for mammals including deer, fisher, coyotes and otters. Its spruce forest supports birds such as golden-crowned kinglets and sharp-shinned hawks, while its grasslands provide important habitat for bobolinks and Savannah sparrows.From Indigenous land to a farming islandAccording to Babson Historical Society, Indigenous communities in the region had established agricultural settlements and maintained a mixed subsistence economy based on farming, fishing, hunting and shellfish gathering. The Agawam and other Indigenous communities used the coastal landscape and surrounding estuaries long before the Crane family arrived, while the islands later became part of a farming landscape that remained important through the 18th and 19th centuries.European settlers later called Choate Island “Hog Island”, reflecting its role in the region’s colonial farming system. The Choate family became closely associated with the island after Thomas Choate acquired land there in the late 17th century, with subsequent generations developing and maintaining farms for generations. The Choate House, built in the early to mid-18th century, became the centre of the family’s long presence. Choate Island and neighbouring Long Island were connected by a causeway, allowing people, livestock and agricultural goods to move between them, while fields, grazing areas, stone walls and farm buildings developed alongside salt marshes and tidal waters. The island was officially renamed Choate Island in 1887.The Cranes arriveThe Trustees of Reservations also note that the next major change came in the early 20th century, when Richard T. Crane Jr., the Chicago industrialist who was developing the Crane Estate around Castle Hill, acquired the first portion of Choate Island in 1917. The Crane family expanded its holdings in 1927, bringing more of the island into the estate. Rather than removing every trace of its agricultural past, the Cranes retained historic structures, including the Choate House and the nearby Proctor Barn on Long Island, while reshaping parts of the landscape for their own use.One of the most visible changes was tree planting, with Cornelius Crane establishing about 95 acres of spruce and pine forest on Choate Island in the 1930s. Norway spruce became one of the dominant species, creating a prominent new feature in the island’s landscape. Over the decades, however, severe storms damaged large sections of the ageing plantation, prompting The Trustees to remove about 30 acres of trees and restore the area as shrubland and young forest habitat. Crane and his wife, Miné, also developed a strong personal connection with the island, using the White Cottage, designed by architect Royal Barry Wills, as a private retreat overlooking Ipswich Bay and the surrounding marshes. The couple were later buried near the island’s summit, where their graves overlook the landscape that had become an important part of their lives.From private estate to wildlife refugeAccording to Historic Massachusetts, Miné Crane donated about 700 acres of land, including Choate Island and surrounding islands and salt marshes, to The Trustees of Reservations in 1974 in memory of her husband, Cornelius Crane. The gift formed the foundation of the Crane Wildlife Refuge, which was later expanded through additional acquisitions and donations. The transition from private estate to protected refuge did not mean freezing the landscape in its historic state. Instead, conservation work has continued to respond to changing ecological conditions. In 2017, for example, The Trustees and conservation partners cleared about 30 acres of ageing Norway spruce plantation after severe storms had damaged large sections of the forest. The project created space for shrubland and young forest habitat, supporting species including American black ducks, American woodcocks, eastern towhees and native pollinators. This approach reflects a broader conservation goal: maintaining a functioning coastal ecosystem rather than preserving every element of the landscape exactly as the Cranes left it. Today, visitors can follow gravel roads and mown trails past the historic Choate House towards the Crane burial site near the island’s highest point. The route passes through a changing landscape of grassland, woodland, shoreline and salt marsh, showing how natural habitats and historic features coexist on the island.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
