articles.title: How a family reunion in China ended in a 3-year prison term for artist Gao Zhen
articles.summary: China News: A family visit to China back in August 2024 ended with a three-year prison sentence for a US-based Chinese artist. Gao Zhen, a member of the artistic .
articles.body: A family visit to China back in August 2024 ended with a three-year prison sentence for a US-based Chinese artist. Gao Zhen, a member of the artistic duo the Gao brothers, was given the prison sentence over a satirical artwork involving statues of Mao Zedong.Gao was sentenced on Tuesday by the Sanhei People's Court in northern Hebei province for âinfringing upon the reputation of heroesâ, according to his wife, Zhao Yaliang. The offence relates to artworks that Chinese authorities consider insulting to revolutionary figures.The sentence brought an abrupt end to hopes that Gao, who has remained in official custody since his arrest, would soon be released and return to his family in the US. Zhao said she had prepared clothes for her husband, expecting that he might be freed.âI felt two years was my limit, and I was really disappointed and sad. I haven't been able to catch my breath,â she said.Gao was arrested while visiting family in China in August 2024, after travelling back from the US, where he and his family had immigrated. He has remained in custody for about two years since then.The case centres on several of Gao's satirical works, including Maoâs Guilt, a 2009 statue depicting Mao Zedong, the founder of modern China, kneeling in repentance. Another is the Miss Mao series, which caricatures Mao with breasts and an exaggerated nose.Gao's supporters say the works predate the law under which he was prosecuted. Shane Yi, a researcher at Chinese Human Rights Defenders who has advocated for the artist, said Gao plans to appeal.Yi described the case as âa very clear case of a violation of a personâs freedom of expression.âThe court did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Amnesty International also criticised the conviction, saying the sentence was intended to discourage artists from challenging official narratives. Gao was handed the maximum three-year prison term available under the offence.âThe lengthy pre-trial detention and, ultimately, decision to convict Gao Zhen and sentence him to the maximum three-year prison term under this offence illustrate the authoritiesâ determination to deter others from engaging in independent artistic expression,â said Amnesty's China Director Sarah Brooks.âNo artist should face criminal punishment for creating work that challenges official narratives or encourages critical reflection on history,â she said.The Gao Brothers became internationally known for works examining authoritarianism and censorship. Their art was exhibited in China and abroad during a period of relative openness in the country.That space for political expression has narrowed in recent years, particularly when artists and others have addressed prominent political figures. China passed a law in 2018 banning criticism of the nation's âheroesâ, which authorities have since used in cases involving depictions of revolutionary figures.For Zhao, however, the case remains deeply personal. She said she hopes to be reunited with her husband and return with him to the US. Chinese courts often count time spent in pre-trial detention as time served towards a prison sentence.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: UN rejects Israel’s threat to expel Gaza residents over kite-flying
articles.summary: UN rights office spokesperson slams Israeli threat of forced evacuations from Gaza communities over kite flying.
articles.body:
The United Nations has condemned Israel's threat to expel Palestinians from areas of the besieged Gaza Strip where kites were being flown by children.

"On the threat of expulsion due to children's kite flying, I hope we can all agree that this is outrageous," UN rights office spokeswoman Ravina Shamdasani told reporters on Tuesday.

Israel warned Hamas on Sunday that it would intensify military operations if kites, drones or balloons continue, saying those responsible would be targeted.

Several kites not carrying incendiary devices were reported to have drifted into southern Israeli communities over the last month. The incidents have evoked memories of incendiary kites and balloons launched from Gaza in 2018, in what Palestinians said was a protest against the Israeli blockade of the enclave.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz, in a joint statement on Sunday, said "Israel warns Hamas that if the launches toward Israel do not cease immediately", Israeli forces "will take action to intensify targeted operations against those responsible". They "will evacuate the population from areas from which kites, drones and balloons are launched", it added.

Gaza's popular committees, coordinating with Hamas authorities, urged parents on Monday to stop children flying kites, saying they were acting "to protect their innocent lives".

"Every summer, my kid, Ahmed, and the kids in the street fly those kites to entertain themselves," Umm Mohammed, a mother in Gaza City, told the Reuters news agency. "But [now] I will not allow him to – not any more."

Basem Naim, a member of Hamas's political bureau, rejected the Israeli warning over the kites.

"Is it conceivable that attempts to appease the war criminal Netanyahu have led them to describe innocent children's activities as armed activities, while Netanyahu continues to kill and destroy daily despite the agreement?"

The dispute comes amid a "ceasefire" in Gaza that has failed to halt Israeli attacks. More than 1,280 Palestinians have been killed since the agreement took effect in October, according to Gaza's Ministry of Health.

articles.summary: News News: Indiaâs house price growth slowed to 3.6 per cent year-on-year in the first quarter of FY27, from 4.5 per cent in the previous quarter, indicating a m.
articles.body: Indiaâs house price growth slowed to 3.6 per cent year-on-year in the first quarter of FY27, from 4.5 per cent in the previous quarter, indicating a moderation in the pace of residential property price increases, according to Reserve Bank of India (RBI) data released this week.The RBIâs All-India House Price Index (HPI) rose to 117.5 in Q1 FY27, from 116.2 in Q4 FY26 and 113.4 in the year-ago quarter. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, the index increased 1.1 per cent.While prices continued to rise, the slower annual growth suggests that the sharp momentum seen in some housing markets has eased. The RBI said the latest annual growth was mainly contributed by Chandigarh, Jaipur, Kanpur, Lucknow and Thiruvananthapuram.âThe HPI registered an annual growth of 3.6 per cent in Q1:2026-27, same as in Q1 of previous year, mainly contributed by the cities such as Chandigarh, Jaipur, Kanpur, Lucknow and Thiruvananthapuram,â the RBI said.Why did house price growth slow?The moderation in the overall index came despite continued quarterly gains in several cities. The RBI said the 1.1 per cent quarter-on-quarter increase was primarily driven by Chandigarh, Lucknow and Thiruvananthapuram.âThe All India HPI increased by 1.1 per cent and stood at 117.5 in Q1:2026-27 compared to previous quarter, primarily driven by an increase in the index for cities such as Chandigarh, Lucknow, and Thiruvananthapuram,â the central bank said.The data therefore points to a mixed housing market, with prices continuing to move higher but the pace of annual appreciation remaining modest. The 3.6% annual growth in Q1 FY27 was also unchanged from the corresponding quarter of FY26.The HPI is compiled quarterly using transaction-level data from property registration authorities. With 2022-23 as the base year, the latest index covers 18 major cities, including Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru, Chennai, Kolkata, Hyderabad, Pune, Ahmedabad and Gurugram-region markets such as Ghaziabad and Gautam Buddha Nagar.The index tracks movements in residential property prices based on registered housing transactions across these cities and provides a broad indicator of the direction of Indiaâs housing market.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: In the 1960s, Takao Shitoâs family refused to surrender its farm for Japanâs Narita Airport; over 50 years later, a runway still bends around his fields
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Explore the incredible story of Takao Shito, a farmer who refused to sell his family's land for Narita International Airport, shaping its runway's design in the process. Discover his ongoing battle against urban development and the legacy of resistance.
articles.body: In the fields surrounding Narita International Airport, jets pass overhead every few minutes as they climb toward Tokyo. Down below, a farmer named Takao Shito tends rows of carrots, onions and radishes on land his family had worked for nearly a century by the time the airport dispute began. His father refused to leave the land in the 1960s, helping force planners to route one runway around the farm.The dispute began in 1966, when the Japanese government chose Sanrizuka, a rural area about 40 miles from Tokyo, as the site for a new international airport intended to symbolise the country's postwar progress. Local farmers, including Shito's father, resisted fiercely from the outset, and the standoff eventually escalated into violence. The feature outlet Japan Insides says the Shito family farmed the same plot for nearly a century, growing rice and vegetables and raising livestock before the government claimed the surrounding land in the 1960s.Decades of clashes over the landDemonstrations against the airport grew increasingly bitter through the late 1960s and 1970s, and at least a dozen police officers and protesters died in the confrontations that followed. Authorities eventually took over many properties, and the number of resisting farms gradually shrank as families accepted compensation and moved elsewhere. Narita finally opened in 1978, though continued local opposition meant that it initially operated with only one runway. Shito was reportedly offered a large payment to give up the land, but he refused.Shito has told the BBC that he is not interested in money and simply wants to continue farming, even though his fields are surrounded by airport infrastructure and aircraft noise. When the airport later built a second runway, planners had already bought the surrounding lots from their legal owners, some of whom had rented land to the Shito family for generations. Shito refused to sell his own portion, pointing to protections under Japan's Agricultural Land Act, and the airport ultimately redesigned the runway so that it curves around his fields rather than passing straight through them.A shrinking village inside an airportWhere roughly 28 households once farmed in Shito's village before construction began, only a handful remain today, and Shito is now the last resident still living inside the airport perimeter itself. Today, he reaches his fields through underground tunnels beneath the taxiways, works amid the roar of aircraft and sells his organic produce directly to regular customers in the Tokyo area. He has often said that the soil, cultivated by three generations of his family for nearly a century before the airport dispute, is too good to abandon. The government has so far chosen not to compel the sale of the last occupied plots, wary that doing so would reignite the unrest that once defined the area. Shito, now in his seventies, continues to farm each day with help from volunteers who bring food and supplies, including former student protesters from decades past.His fight has become a symbol of the broader Sanrizuka land dispute, one of modern Japanâs longest-running social movements.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: South Korean president calls for greater police accountability after Jeju missing-person cases
articles.summary: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung called for greater police accountability after public outrage over the handling of a series of missing-person cases on Jeju island.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — South Korean President Lee Jae Myung called for greater police accountability after public outrage over the handling of a series of missing-person cases on Jeju island, as reforms are set to give the force a bigger role in criminal investigations. “Police are likely to wield the greatest power among state institutions,” Lee told a cabinet meeting Tuesday, adding that the public questioned whether the force could bear the responsibility. “Responsibility must be strengthened in proportion to the size of the authority.” Four people reported missing on Jeju were found dead over three days through Monday, authorities said. The cases were unrelated, but two had allegedly been closed by the same officer without confirmation that the missing people were safe. The allegations have prompted police to review all 298 missing-person reports handled by the officer. About 10 are being examined for possible improper closure, media reported. One case involved Jang Mi-ran, a 37-year-old woman whose disappearance became a national controversy after police allegedly closed the case without confirming her safety. Her body was found on Monday, 104 days after she vanished. The other involved a man in his 60s whose family reported him missing again, prompting a renewed search that ended with his body being found. A court detained the officer Tuesday on suspicion of dereliction of duty, falsifying official electronic records and obstructing official duties, the Yonhap news agency reported. The officer denied the charges and said he contacted the missing people, the report said, citing a police official. Jeju police told Reuters they had no separate comment on their handling of the cases, which has fueled safety concerns and criticism on social media. Acting National Police Commissioner Yoo Jae-seong apologized and promised measures to prevent a recurrence. Police have ordered supervisory sign-off on missing-person case closures pending an upgrade to their case management system, Yoo told lawmakers Monday. “We will examine the entire system and make institutional improvements so that this never happens again,” Yoo said, pledging to review all cases handled by the officer. South Korean police received 70,814 reports of missing adults last year, official data showed. More than 70,000 such reports have been filed annually since 2022, though the vast majority were solved within 30 days, police say. The controversy comes after the governing Democratic Party stripped prosecutors of their remaining investigative powers in July, citing a history of abuse. The change, due to take effect in October, leaves police with a greatly expanded investigative role.

articles.title: Nepal flash floods: Heavy casualties feared
articles.summary: The flood in Rasuwa - an area north of Kathmandu bordering Tibet - is feared to have swept away villages.
articles.body:
Heavy casualties are feared after a massive flash flood and mudslide along the Tibet-Nepal border washed away villages and damaged roads and infrastructure.

The flood hit early on Wednesday in Rasuwa, just north of Nepal's capital Kathmandu. It was reportedly caused by excessive snow melting into the Bhote Koshi river that flows from Tibet to Nepal.

Twelve people have been rescued so far, and search operations are under way on both sides of the border, with several areas downstream on high alert.

State media in China, which controls Tibet, say there are significant casualties. Nepalese officials anticipate "huge scale loss" and posted videos showing floodwater crashing through villages.

Roads, communications and power in the region have been disrupted and the authorities say the main road to Kathmandu is closed.

"Our logistics company has seven container trucks there, all staffed by Nepalese employees. We have lost contact with all of them. There is no signal, so we cannot reach anyone," Yee Liang, a Chinese businessman based in Kathmandu, told the BBC.

"As far as I know, there was no warning. There were occasional mudslides and landslides, especially in the rainy season, but this one seems much more serious."

The extent of the damage on the Tibetan side is unclear but the BBC spoke to Guan Daoxuan in Sichuan province who said he had lost contact with his wife late on Wednesday morning.

She works for a state-run construction company involved in building roads and bridges in Tibet. Guan said Nepalese authorities had tried to send a helicopter to inspect the area because road access had been cut off, but strong winds were making it difficult for the aircraft to reach the site.

Nepal's disaster management authority called on people living near river banks in vulnerable areas to remain alert and take precautions.

"Work has started to take necessary steps in coordination with the medical team, scouts, and Red Cross," Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in a social media post, after holding an emergency meeting to take stock of the situation.

Authorities said 13 officers from the armed police force were missing from two posts in Rasuwa district, and they had not been able to contact dozens of other police officers.

Rasuwa saw deadly flooding last year that killed 18 people after a glacier burst on the Chinese side of the border.

Officials have told the BBC that they believe the scale of Wednesday's disaster exceeds last year's floods.

articles.title: Big heels, bigger wigs: Dolly Parton’s singular style
articles.summary: The late Dolly Parton often flirted with bad taste, styling plunging necklines with long acrylic nails and heapings of glitter. But she paired it with charm and a keen sense of self-awareness that only made her fans love her more.
articles.body: Adorned in rhinestones and elevating her 5-foot stature with sky-high heels and voluminous blonde wigs, Dolly Parton often joked, “it costs a lot of money to look this cheap!” Parton’s looks on stage and off reflected both her Tennessee roots and her embodiment of over-the-top feminine glamour, an aesthetic articulated in her album title and self-anointed nickname “Backwoods Barbie.” She was rarely seen without long acrylic nails, a full face of makeup, and heapings of glitter. The prolific musician, actor and philanthropist, who died on Tuesday at 80 years old, always had a tongue-in-cheek response to criticisms about her larger-than-life sense of style. She quipped about her hair being a fire hazard, would play her hit ‘9 to 5’ with nothing but her fire red acrylic nails as the instrument, and she unabashedly loved flashy clothes: shoulder pads, plunging necklines, a cinched waist, lace were all sartorial non-negotiables for the singer. But she paired it with a keen sense of self-awareness that only made her devout fanbase love her more. “When I moved to Nashville in 1964, I already had some ideas about what I wanted to look like onstage — and off,” she wrote in her book “Behind the Seams” in 2023. “Country stars had to have big hair and some sparkles, and you had to have a Cadillac. I had the big hair but not yet the Cadillac — or enough sparkles.” She related to the clothes worn by famous fixtures on stage of the Grand Ole Opry, like Jean Shepard and didn’t shy away from the unconventional things that influenced her, telling People she even took inspiration from the famously risqué Frederick’s of Hollywood catalogs she flipped through when she was young. Parton’s version of glamour wasn’t afraid to flirt with bad taste. “I want to look a little bit, you know, trashy,” she said last year. “I don’t mean it in a bad way. I just like that kind of almost artificial look. I like the overdone. I like the bleached hair.” Persuasive style Parton’s conviction was the backbone of her persona, and she recalled in “Behind the Seams” that when she first signed to Monument Records in 1965, the label president wanted to “flatten” her hair and dress her in “streamlined” clothes more fitting of ’60s pop stars. “But I hated everything about it. I felt naked,” she said. Even her softer looks had volume, such as Parton’s cover for her 1973 chart-topping album “Jolene,” in stripes and billowing white shoulders and with her blonde mane framing her face. But on stage and on red carpets she gravitated towards hot pink jumpsuits, icy blue off-shoulder gowns or pearl-encrusted cropped jackets. She worked with designers like Bob Mackie, who created a wing-like “Butterfly” gown for her TV special “Dolly & Carol in Nashville” in 1979, and dressed her and Oprah in complimentary looks for Parton’s variety show “Dolly.” In 2000, she attended a White House luncheon to talk about her book gifting charity Imagination Library in a vibrant, fringed yellow skirt suit with matching heels. Fringe was another Parton trademark. Her looks often incorporated classic country motifs like cowboy hats or bell-bottom jeans, though usually made Dolly-appropriate with a healthy helping of sparkles and vibrant hues. Parton wore some 300 custom outfits a year, styled by her longtime collaborator Steve Summers. He told Vogue that everything was custom for Parton, even if started as an off-the-rack dress. “There is an outfit in production every single day,” he said. “If she’s doing personal appearances, 10 outfits in a day is not unusual.” Many stars have borrowed from Parton over the years: her goddaughter Miley Cyrus has appeared with her in synchronized outfits; Beyoncé has channeled her for her own take on “Jolene;” and Sabrina Carpenter has dueted with her, too, leaning into the unapologetic femininity (and butter-yellow curls) that made Parton an icon. But Parton’s style is something anyone can slip on, and her fans have often played dress-up with her, too. The British photographer Alice Hawkins spent a decade documenting herself and others living out their own Dolly-fied American dreams in her image, published in the book “Dear Dolly” in 2022. Parton even once joined the fun by entering a Dolly lookalike contest at a West Hollywood gay bar — which she lost. “I say it’s a good thing I was a girl or I’d be a drag queen,” she said in an interview recounting the episode. And though guests who make the pilgrimage to her Tennessee theme park Dollywood may not dress as her — per the official rules, since she herself often attended — many still pay small tributes to her style with a touch of glitz. Parton may have had a replicable sartorial style, but the core of it was a message that anyone could adopt, bedazzled or not: “I’m gonna be me, ‘cause I know who I am and you don’t.”

articles.title: In 2002, Lundy began removing invasive rats; 11 years later, Manx shearwater pairs had risen from 300 to 3,000
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Conservation groups began a campaign to remove invasive rats from Lundy, a rocky island in the Bristol Channel in 2002. Ten years later, surveys found.
articles.body: Conservation groups began a campaign to remove invasive rats from Lundy, a rocky island in the Bristol Channel in 2002. Ten years later, surveys found about 3,000 breeding pairs of Manx shearwaters, up from roughly 300 when the recovery project began. Guillemots were also using breeding sites on cliffs and areas that had previously been accessible to rats. The project was launched because rats were preying on seabird eggs and chicks. Lundy had suitable nesting habitat, but several bird populations had fallen sharply. The removal effort eventually made the island rat-free, and subsequent surveys recorded increases across several seabird species. The same basic problem is being tackled on islands thousands of miles away. In the Marshall Islands, a rat-eradication campaign completed in 2024 was followed by the return of thousands of native seedlings and a colony of about 2,000 sooty terns within a year.Why rats became a problem on LundyRecords cited by the Lundy Bird Observatory say both brown rats and black rats were present, and the animals were known to prey on seabirds, their eggs and young. That mattered particularly for burrow-nesting species, since Manx shearwaters spend much of their lives at sea but return to land to breed, and use underground burrows to raise their chicks. The seabird recovery project brought together Natural England, the RSPB, the National Trust and the Landmark Trust. Its objective was to remove the rats and give nesting seabirds a better chance of reproducing successfully.The eradication operation itself ran from November 2002 to March 2004, with work concentrated during two winters. The timing was chosen because natural food available to rats was lower during winter, increasing the likelihood that they would take the bait. Lundy was later confirmed rat-free, with the island formally declared free of rats in 2006. When RSPB survey teams returned in 2013, they found that the number of breeding Manx shearwater pairs had risen from 300 to 3,000. Puffins had increased from five birds to 80, while razorbills and shags had also recorded gains.Guillemots began using more of the cliffsLundy Bird Observatory records show that guillemots were breeding at the island after the rat eradication, with their numbers rising substantially in later surveys. In 2013, researchers recorded 4,114 individual guillemots at breeding colonies, compared with 3,302 in 2008. The observatory also noted that guillemots had begun appearing at new breeding sites in areas of broken ground close to the grassy slopes. Those locations had previously been relatively accessible to rats.The evidence does not mean every change in the guillemot population can be attributed to rat removal, since food availability and other environmental factors also affect seabird numbers. The observatory describes the role of rat removal as a likely factor rather than the sole explanation. By 2021, the breeding census recorded 6,198 guillemots at Lundy, the highest total in the regular survey record at that point. Breeding was confirmed again in subsequent monitoring. The Manx shearwater population also continued to rise well beyond the 2013 survey. A later RSPB-led census estimated 12,638 apparently occupied nesting sites in 2023, equivalent to more than 25,000 individual birds.A similar result appeared in the Marshall IslandsConservationists were dealing with the same type of problem on Bikar Atoll and Jemo Islet in the Republic of the Marshall Islands more than 7,000 miles from Lundy. In 2024, the Marshall Islands government and conservation partners carried out a campaign to remove invasive rats from the two islands. Island Conservation provided technical support as part of the wider Pacific Regional Invasive Species Management Support Service program.In 2025, conservationists reported a colony of about 2,000 sooty terns on Bikar Atoll, where no such colony had been recorded during the previous monitoring. The birds were feeding hundreds of chicks. Conservation teams counted thousands of native Pisonia grandis seedlings across 60 monitored 12-by-12-meter plots. In 2024, they had found none in those plots. Island Conservation's report also notes that Jemo had traditionally been used by people from nearby Likiep Atoll to gather natural resources. Rats had reduced those resources, including coconut crabs, so the restoration effort was intended to have practical benefits for nearby communities as well as ecological ones.The two projects differ in scale, geography and methods, but their monitoring has produced a similar sequence: remove an introduced predator, then watch what happens to species that had been struggling in its presence. In Lundy, the changes have continued for more than two decades. The island now supports tens of thousands of breeding seabirds, while the Marshall Islands project is only beginning its longer-term monitoring. For both sites, the next challenge is keeping rats from returning and tracking whether the early gains persist.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Two dead and warehouse ablaze in Russia after Ukrainian drone strikes
articles.summary: Two people have been killed in a new wave of Ukrainian drone strikes on targets in Russia, news agency Interfax reported on Wednesday, citing officials. The...
articles.body:
Two people have been killed in a new wave of Ukrainian drone strikes on targets in Russia, news agency Interfax reported on Wednesday, citing officials.

The governor of Russia's Lipetsk region, Igor Artamonov, said a man and a 14-year-old girl were killed after a drone crashed into their house, setting it on fire, according to Interfax.

The Defence Ministry in Moscow said on Wednesday that 426 Ukrainian drones had been intercepted and destroyed overnight.

The capital was also among the targets, while airports in Tambov, Nizhny Novgorod and Yaroslavl temporarily suspended take-offs and landings due to air raid alerts.

In the Tambov region, some 600 kilometres south-east of Moscow, a warehouse belonging to the major Russian online retailer Wildberries was targeted. The drone attack caused a fire at the warehouse in Kotovsk, which spread to 100,000 square metres, the region's governor, Yevgeny Pervyshov, said.

Strikes were also launched at Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014. Three Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missiles were intercepted over the Black Sea, the Moscow-installed governor of the port city of Sevastopol, Mikhail Razvozhaev, wrote on social media.

articles.title: Spain's 'brown challenge': Kids defecating in pools for likes online
articles.summary: Spain's public swimming pools are being hit by a revolting and unhygienic social media trend in which children and teenagers deliberately defecate in pools s...
articles.body:
Spain's public swimming pools are being hit by a revolting and unhygienic social media trend in which children and teenagers deliberately defecate in pools so they can film the ensuing chaos for views and likes online.

The trend, known as the reto marrón ("brown challenge"), is causing widespread outrage and significant damage at outdoor pools across the country, local media report.

Although fines can reach €20,000, in addition to substantial compensation claims and multi-year bans, Spanish media are reporting new cases almost daily.

There is no central record of incidents at the mostly municipally run pools, but there were around 300 last year and already "hundreds" so far this year, broadcaster Cadena Ser reported.

Catching perpetrators in the act is difficult, however. Some reportedly bring faeces in plastic bags hidden in their swimwear and empty them into the water, the newspaper La Razón reported.

In the northern Spanish city of Burgos, however, fine proceedings have now been launched against the parents of four children aged between 11 and 13, the city administration confirmed to dpa. They were seen by an adult releasing faeces in the El Plantío pool. The man immediately alerted police, who took down the children's details.

The parents now face fines of €3,000 ($3,500) each and compensation claims from the municipality for cleaning and disinfecting the pool. If the water has to be replaced, this can cost several thousand euros. The perpetrators themselves also face multi-year bans.

Burgos mayor Cristina Ayala stressed that proceedings would be pursued "to the very end." She said it was already the sixth such case at the city's outdoor pools this year.

Andrés López, a psychiatrist and coordinator for mental health in the Osuna health district, said in an interview with Cadena Ser that this type of behaviour could stem from emotional problems in a particularly vulnerable group such as teenagers and young adults.

He said they use social media to seek recognition or to combat feelings of loneliness. López stressed that social media have certain addictive mechanisms that encourage a bandwagon effect, leading people to imitate this kind of antisocial behaviour.

articles.title: Australia charges man with trying to pass Ukrainian military intel to Russia
articles.summary: The crime of intentional foreign interference carries a penalty of 20 years' imprisonment in Australia.
articles.body:
Australian police said on Friday that a man has been charged with foreign interference for allegedly seeking to inform Russia about Ukrainian military activities.

The 27-year-old Russian-Australian citizen had "military style" training in Russia and later joined the Ukrainian armed forces, Australian Federal Police commissioner Krissy Barrett said at a news conference.

"We don't want Australia to become a safe haven for people who are undertaking foreign interference on behalf of other countries," she said.

Police alleged he travelled to Russia for the training in October 2024.

He then returned to Australia, they say, where he "maintained contact" with individuals he believed were linked to Russian intelligence.

Police allege he travelled to Ukraine in 2025 where he enlisted in the country's armed forces and "gained access to information relating to their military personnel, units and locations."

He then "provided, or attempted to provide, information obtained in Ukraine to individuals he believed were acting on behalf of Russian intelligence services," Barrett said.

"It is alleged this conduct created a risk to the safety and security of Ukrainian military personnel."

The crime of intentional foreign interference carries a penalty of 20 years' imprisonment in Australia.

Ukraine has been fighting against Russia's full-scale invasion since it was launched in February 2022.

"We have committed over $1.5 billion (€900 million) to help Ukraine defend itself, including more than $1.3 billion (€700 million) in military support through vital equipment for the battlefield and the training of Ukrainian forces, " Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong said in February last year .

"Australia has been clear since day one that Russia, and those enabling its illegal invasion, will face consequences."

articles.title: In 2024, Marshall Islands crews cleared rats from two remote islands: A year later, 2,000 sooty terns returned
articles.summary: US News: Conservation teams spread rat bait across Bikar Atoll and Jemo Islet in the Marshall Islands using drones in July 2024. A year later, monitoring teams.
articles.body: Conservation teams spread rat bait across Bikar Atoll and Jemo Islet in the Marshall Islands using drones in July 2024. A year later, monitoring teams found a new colony of about 2,000 sooty terns on Bikar and thousands of native tree seedlings across the forest floor. Invasive rats had overrun the two remote islands for years. The rodents ate native vegetation, seabird eggs and young, turtle hatchlings and other wildlife. On Jemo, they also damaged resources traditionally collected by people from the nearby Likiep Atoll. The Marshall Islands government led the restoration effort, with technical support from Island Conservation. By 2025, monitoring indicated that the rats had been successfully removed from both islands.The rats had taken over the forest floorIsland Conservation project manager Paul Jacques visited Bikar and Jemo in 2024, when rats were widespread across both islands. He told CNN that the animals were running through the forest at night and had become a major pressure on native species. The problem was particularly serious for animals that nest or feed on the ground. Rats can eat eggs and young birds, while also consuming seeds and seedlings before they can develop into mature plants.CNN reported that the bait was dropped by drone in July 2024 at a rate of about 25 kilograms per hectare. The pellets were distributed in lines across the islands so that rats would have little opportunity to avoid them. The campaign was carried out with the Marshall Islands Marine Resources Authority and the Ministry of Natural Resources and Commerce. The goal was to remove the invasive predator and allow the existing ecosystem to recover.A new seabird colony appeared within a yearWhen conservationists returned in 2025, they found about 2,000 sooty terns breeding on Bikar. There had been no sooty terns recorded there during the previous year's monitoring. Conservationists also observed greater crested terns and brown noddies nesting on the ground. A Christmas shearwater was recorded on Bikar, while geckos and land crabs that had not been detected during the 2024 visit were also seen.Island Conservation's September 2025 report said the sooty tern colony was feeding hundreds of chicks. The organization described the findings as evidence that the 2024 rat-removal campaign had succeeded. The result is notable because sooty terns are vulnerable to predators when they nest on the ground. Removing rats does not automatically guarantee a population increase, but the new colony appeared during the first year after eradication. The monitoring team used trail cameras, traps, spotlight searches and thermal detection equipment to check whether rats remained on the islands. Those methods supported the conclusion that the rodents had been successfully eradicated.The forest floor changed just as quicklyConservationists found thousands of seedlings of the native Pisonia grandis tree on monitored plots across the islands. In 2024, none had been recorded in the 60 monitored plots. Pisonia grandis is important to island ecosystems because mature trees provide habitat used by seabirds. The sudden appearance of young plants therefore matters beyond the number of seedlings counted. The change also suggests that seeds were surviving after the rats were removed. Before the eradication, rats could consume seeds and young plants before they had a chance to establish themselves.Island Conservation reported that the recovery was documented by teams from the organization, the Marshall Islands Marine Resources Authority, the Ministry of Natural Resources and Commerce and community members from Utrik Atoll. The restoration also has a connection to the surrounding ocean. Seabirds carry nutrients from the sea onto islands through their guano, which adds nutrients to the soil, and those nutrients can support plant growth and eventually move back into nearby marine ecosystems. The Marshall Islands' Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme said the 2024 rat-removal project was part of the Predator Free Pacific program, with Island Conservation providing technical expertise. The program involved both Bikar and Jemo and was led locally by Marshall Islands agencies.Jemo could become useful to nearby communities againJemo Islet lies about 40 kilometers from Likiep Atoll. CNN reported that people from Likiep have traditionally traveled to Jemo to fish, collect coconut crabs and gather plants such as coconuts and pandan leaves used for weaving. Those resources had declined as invasive rats became established, and the restoration project was therefore not limited to wildlife protection. Local communities also have an interest in keeping Jemo free of rats so that its natural resources can recover.Bikar is rarely visited outside scientific expeditions, while visitors to Jemo will need to avoid accidentally bringing rats or other invasive species back. There are also plans to assess whether similar work could be carried out elsewhere. Island Conservation said feasibility studies were underway for Bokak Atoll, another remote Marshall Islands ecosystem where invasive rats remain a problem.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: How Dolly Parton became the one thing most Americans could agree on
articles.summary: The cultural icon was one of the rare celebrities adored by Americans of all ages, races and political persuasions.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton was a lot of things - a country musician, a philanthropist, an actress, a storyteller and a businesswoman. One thing she never was, however, was a politician.

But don't think it's because no one asked her. In 1999, during an appearance on the talk show Prime Time Country!, the singer was asked by a young woman in the audience if she would ever run for office.

Dolly demurred, with her characteristic razor-sharp wit. "I think of myself more as a diplomat. That's the kind of people who tell you to go to hell in such a way you look forward to the trip."

It's something she'd had to do many times over a career that spanned decades and genres. With a fanbase that included grandmas and Gen-Zers, Republicans and Democrats, drag queens and evangelicals, Parton was a kind of unicorn in America's polarised society.

"She is the one person who straddles political dividesâ¦ the so-called culture wars," said Sarah Phillips, who teaches an Anthropology of Dolly Parton course at Indiana University - and still finds it hard to speak about the singer in the past tense. The professor "curled into a ball" in her office and "just sobbed" upon hearing of the death.

A recent poll by YouGov said that Parton's net approval rating was 65% - compared with Barack Obama's 14%, Taylor Swift's 3%, Donald Trump's -19% and Joe Biden's -18%.

Much of that universal appeal has been attributed to Parton's steadfast refusal to weigh into politics, for fear of alienating her fans.

"I've got as many Republican fans as Democrats and I don't want to make any of them mad at me, so I don't play politics," she once said during an interview with Fox News.

She turned down the Presidential Medal of Freedom from two different presidents. She twice declined Donald Trump's offer, citing scheduling and health reasons. So when Joe Biden offered it to her a few years later, she felt she had to decline as well, otherwise it would look like she had a preference for one over the other.

Elton John, Oprah Winfrey and Paul McCartney lead tributes to Parton Published 3 hours ago

Elton John, Oprah Winfrey and Paul McCartney lead tributes to Parton

How Parton told her life story through six iconic songs Published 9 hours ago

How Parton told her life story through six iconic songs

After news broke on Tuesday of Parton's death, tributes poured in from politicians from both sides. Trump ordered American flags to be flown at half mast - an honour usually reserved for elite statesmen and judges.

"There has never been anyone like her, and never will," Trump wrote on social media.

In her own social media post, Hillary Clinton wrote "she was the best of America".

Even though she avoided partisan politics, Parton was never apolitical - speaking about subjects including women's rights, LGBTQ equality and Black Lives Matter .

That commitment to speaking her mind, and her "amazing sense of self", Phillips said, was integral to Parton's near-universal appeal and self-styled diplomacy.

"She has always been a model for women, carving your own path, looking out for yourself, making sure that you retain the rights to your intellectual property, looking out for your own financial and creative independence," Phillips told the BBC.

"And if that's not feminism, I don't know what is."

Public interest in Parton's views began many years ago, when she made it clear to anyone listening that she was not a cookie-cutter country singer.

In 1977, she became a crossover pop sensation, but instead of alienating her base, she grew her audience. Then, in 1980, she made her film debut in 9 to 5, a dark satire about women's rights in the workplace helped by Jane Fonda. Fonda was persona non-grata in many parts of the country for her anti-Vietnam War activism.

But Parton refused to distance herself from Fonda just to appease her more conservative fans. She said: "I respect anybody's beliefs and the fact that they're willing to stand up for whatever it is. But I'm also the kind of person that if I don't like where you got it, I can tell you where to put it."

After learning of her death, Fonda posted on social media: "She is woven into all our lives and hearts forever."

Parton's image is similarly woven into public minds: always camp, always glamorous, always smiling and always kind. Her aesthetics were deliberately cultivated, another calculated move from a shrewd entrepreneur who understood showbusiness as well as she understood people.

When television journalist Barbara Walters grilled Parton about her looks in a 1977 segment - asking if the singer was a joke - the interviewer arguably met her match.

"Dolly Parton made it very clear that she knows exactly what she's doing," Phillips said, reflecting on how Parton handled the interview.

"This is how she feels comfortable, and she even said [to Walters]: 'Everybody thinks that the joke's on me, but in fact, the joke is on the public. I know very well what I'm doing, and I can change my image any time I want to.'"

Journalists have tried - and failed - over the years to get Parton to go off script. But whenever they asked her to weigh into political terrain, she would pivot like a boxer.

Instead of left-hooks, Parton's main defences were humour and self-deprecation. During a press conference in 2016, she told a gaggle of journalists that "I've been thinking about running myselfâ¦ we could use a few more boobs in the race", and nodded at her chest.

But Parton never did run for office - even though her father, when he was alive, liked to drive around town with a bumper sticker that said "Dolly for President".

Instead she poured her heart and soul into her philanthropy - like her Imagination Library, which sent free books to children around the world, or her work helping to fund the Moderna Covid-19 vaccine .

Her charity came from a deeply personal place.

Parton grew up in abject poverty, raised in a one-bedroom log cabin alongside 11 siblings. When her career took off, she employed much of her family in her business endeavours and spread that wealth to the local Tennessee community.

She bought an ownership stake in an existing theme park in 1986 in the mountains where she grew up, and it was rechristened Dollywood: a resort and enterprise that remains the single largest employer in the county.

Tennessee musician James Rogers, president of the board of the American Eagle Foundation - which joined forces with Dollywood for a bald eagle sanctuary - recalled the singer's unrivalled kindness and one-on-one attentiveness.

"She's even sweeter than you realise," he told the BBC, recalling a time decades ago when Parton arrived for a performance and spotted him to the side with his wife and daughter Heather, who was around 10 years old.

Parton "detoured the whole entourage to come around over there to where we were and then she knelt down to talk to Heather for a minute".

"The truth is, she supports everybody," said Phillips, who grew up in the North Carolina mountains "across the holler" from Parton's Appalachian Tennessee.

The professor spends "a lot of time" in her class exploring Parton's politics - or "Dollitics", a phrase coined by the singer's nephew to describe her way of handling thorny subjects.

Phillips added that Parton was emblematic of the very values America was built upon and still holds dear, namely "independence" and "freedom to do what you want".

"When we think about the American Dream in the sort of old-fashioned sense of - If you're talented, if you work really, really, really hard, you can achieve your dreams - she embodied that very much."

Phillips and and the many people who paid tribute to the late singer all noted how singular Parton was.

"This summer, I was in France, and I was in Poland, and I ask people, who's the Polish Dolly Parton? Who's the French Dolly Parton?" Phillips said.

"And nobody has an answer, because there isn't one."

articles.title: GPS cannot work everywhere, so scientists tested a new navigation system that uses Cosmic rays instead of satellites to make it work under water and rocks
articles.summary: Tech News News: GPS has become essential for navigation. But there is one major limitation: GPS signals cannot travel through water, rocks or deep underground spaces..
articles.body: GPS has become essential for navigation. But there is one major limitation: GPS signals cannot travel through water, rocks or deep underground spaces. To address the problem, scientists in Japan are now testing an alternative navigation system that uses particles from cosmic rays instead of satellites. According to a report by Ars Technica, the system is called the Muometric Wireless Navigation System, or MuWNS. It uses naturally occurring particles known as muons to determine location in places where GPS cannot work, including underground, indoors and underwater.The researchers say the technology could one day help guide robots during search and rescue operations, support autonomous vehicles in underground spaces and improve navigation in places where satellite signals are unavailable.How cosmic rays could help navigation work underground and underwaterCosmic rays constantly produce particles called muons that fall across the Earth. Unlike GPS radio signals, muons can pass through dense materials, including water and large amounts of rock.âCosmic ray muons fall evenly across the Earth and always travel at the same speed no matter what material they pass through, penetrating even kilometers of rock,â Hiroyuki Tanaka of the University of Tokyo said.âNow, using muons, weâve developed a new type of GPS, which weâve called muPS, that works underground, indoors, and underwater.âThe technology works by using reference stations placed above ground along with a receiver that detects muons below the surface. By measuring the particles and using synchronized clocks, the system can calculate the location of the receiver.Muon technology is not entirely new. Scientists have previously used muons to study volcanoes, examine ancient structures and search for hidden spaces inside pyramids. The Japanese researchers are now exploring whether the same particles can help solve a different problem: navigation without satellite signals.Scientists tested the system by walking through a building basementEarlier versions of the system required the receiver to be connected to a ground station with wires, limiting where it could be used. The new MuWNS system is wireless and uses accurate quartz clocks to synchronize the reference stations and receiver.For a test, researchers placed reference stations on the sixth floor of a building while a person carrying the receiver walked through corridors in the basement. The system tracked the person's route and was able to reconstruct the path taken.The researchers reported an accuracy of between 2 and 25 metres, with a range of up to 100 metres.âThis is as good as, if not better than, single-point GPS positioning over the ground in urban areas,â Tanaka said. However, he added that the technology is still far from being ready for everyday use. âPeople need an accuracy of one meter, and the key to that is time synchronization.âGet the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Japanese engineerâs anime-inspired hair was meant to save time, but it ended up testing a driver safety camera; and now holds more than 250 patents
articles.summary: Rest of World News: For years, one Honda engineer has stood out in a workplace where technical expertise usually gets more attention than appearance. Odateâs stiff, natur.
articles.body: For years, one Honda engineer has stood out in a workplace where technical expertise usually gets more attention than appearance. Odateâs stiff, naturally curly hair falls across his face in a style that has prompted comparisons with famous anime characters, yet the look was never designed to attract attention. He adopted it largely to avoid spending time trying to control his unruly hair. Away from the hairstyle, he has built an impressive career in vehicle safety since joining Honda in 2003.According to South China Morning Post (SCMP), He now leads a team of about 100 engineers and is credited with 253 patents related to safe-driving technology. His unusual appearance has even proved useful at work, when his partly covered eye became an unexpected challenge for a camera system designed to monitor drivers for signs of drowsiness.Japan engineerâs unusual hairstyle draws anime comparisons for a simple reasonOdate has kept the distinctive hairstyle for at least five years. It was not, by his account, the result of trying to imitate an anime character. His hair is naturally stiff and tends to curl, while irregular sleeping habits leave it in a particularly untidy state by morning. When he was younger, he would spend a considerable amount of time trying to make a more conventional haircut behave. Eventually, he stopped fighting it.These days, the routine is considerably simpler. He uses gel to control the section of hair that falls towards his left eye and otherwise lets the rest settle as it will. The result is a look that has drawn comparisons with characters from series such as Naruto and Dragon Ball.At Honda, however, the hairstyle has long since ceased to be a novelty for the people who work with him.The Honda engineer behind 253 patents in safe-driving technologyOdate joined Honda in 2003, beginning his career as a designer working on seat belts. His work later moved towards driver-assistance technology, and he now heads the company's advanced technology development department.The team under his direction numbers roughly 100 people. His work has also led to an unusually large patent portfolio, with 253 patents attributed to him in the field of safe-driving technology.His stated focus has remained fairly straightforward: developing systems intended to protect people in vehicles. His description of the goal is equally spare; the best outcome for a safety system is that nothing happens at all.That approach has also shaped some of the less obvious testing carried out by his team.A hairstyle meant to save time became a test case for safety technologyDuring the development of a camera designed to monitor a driver's eyes, Odate offered himself as a useful test subject. The system was intended to follow eye movements and identify signs that could point to drowsiness or other problems. Odate's fringe, which partly covers his left eye, created a rather practical challenge for the camera.If the system could correctly track an eye that was partly hidden by hair, it provided another way to examine how well the technology performed under less-than-ideal conditions.It was an unusual consequence of a hairstyle that had originally been adopted largely to avoid spending too much time arranging it each morning.Odateâs look has attracted attention from colleagues and rivals alikeOdate's appearance can look particularly striking when set against Honda's standard white workwear. But inside the company, colleagues appear to have become accustomed to it. His professionalism is often mentioned alongside the hairstyle, and his appearance has even become a talking point beyond Honda, with people at other automotive companies reportedly recognising him.He has also appeared at motor shows, where he has presented Honda vehicles and the technology developed by his department.The public-facing appearances have given his unusual look a wider audience, but the attention surrounding him has not been limited to his hair.Odateâs 170kg bench press adds another layer to his unusual public imageOdate also has an interest in strength training. He has said that he exercises every morning, partly as a way of dealing with the pressures that come with his job. His numbers in the gym are striking by ordinary standards. His reported personal best is a 170kg bench press for five consecutive repetitions.That combination of an unconventional hairstyle, a senior engineering role, a long list of patents and a substantial strength-training routine has proved unusually suited to social media.Some online viewers have compared him with the physically imposing characters common in Japanese anime and manga. Others have focused less on the appearance and more on the career behind it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: HAL, Safran seal engine deal to power multi-role choppers

articles.body: BENGALURU: Defence PSU HAL and Safran Helicopter Engines have signed the final contract with their joint venture, Safhal Helicopter Engines Pvt Ltd, to design and develop a new high-power helicopter engine that will power Indiaâs proposed 13-tonne Indian Multi-Role Helicopter (IMRH) and its naval variant Deck-Based Multi-Role Helicopter (DBMRH).The engine, Aravalli, named after Indiaâs iconic mountain range, will be developed in the 3,500-4,000 shaft horsepower (shp) class. The contract covers its design, development, manufacture, supply and lifecycle support.The agreement was signed by HALâs director (engineering and R&D) Ajay Kumar Shrivastava and Olivier Savin, director, Safhal Helicopter Engines and executive vice-president (sales and marketing) at Safran Helicopter Engines.âThe signing of this contract marks a significant step forward in Indiaâs pursuit of self-reliance in aero-engine technologies. Through this collaborative programme with Safhal and Safran Helicopter Engines, weâre creating a strong foundation for powering next-generation Indian helicopter platforms,â HAL CMD Ravi K said.Aravalli will be a new-generation turboshaft engine designed specifically for the IMRH and DBMRH. Safran Helicopter Engines chief executive Cedric Goubet said the programme marked a new phase in the partnership between the two companies.âThis is the first time Safran HE has taken up such a class of engine as co-development. The Aravalli engine programme represents a new chapter in the strategic relationship between France and India, combining the expertise of our teams to develop propulsion systems for future Indian rotorcraft,â Goubet said.HAL and Safran have worked together on helicopter engines for decades. Safranâs Artouste engines powered the Cheetah and Chetak helicopters, while the Shakti engine family powers HALâs Advanced Light Helicopter, Light Combat Helicopter and Light Utility Helicopter.Beyond the two military helicopter programmes â IMRH and DBMRH â Aravalli could also find applications in civil aviation, including offshore transport, utility missions and VVIP travel. The programme is also expected to support the development of maintenance, repair and overhaul capabilities in India.The IMRH programme is central to HALâs plans to develop a medium-lift helicopter to meet the requirements of the Indian armed forces, potentially replacing ageing platforms and reducing dependence on imported helicopters and engines.

articles.title: Far-right Israeli lawmaker damages Palestinian memorial with sledgehammer
articles.summary: Zvi Sukkot's actions have drawn widespread condemnation, including from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
articles.body:
A far-right member of the Israeli parliament has badly damaged a Palestinian memorial with a sledgehammer in the occupied West Bank while under military escort.

The incident has drawn strong criticism from Palestinians and across the political spectrum in Israel.

Video footage showed Zvi Sukkot, a member of the far-right Religious Zionism party, and several others striking the stone memorial in the Palestinian village of Madama.

In the video, Sukkot - who has a history of provocative anti-Palestinian acts - says: "This is something we cannot leave standing here, because any place that glorifies terrorism, we must remove it."

Rami Nasar, the head of the village council in Madama, said that the monument was erected in 2008 to remember Palestinians killed in the battle of Karameh - a day-long military confrontation between Israeli forces and those of both the PLO and Jordan in 1968.

It also memorialises Palestinians killed in the first and second intifada.

Nasar said it was intended to honour those who had been killed in conflict with Israel, whatever their political affiliation.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said its soldiers had been present during the incident. The Israeli military said it had approved a tour of monuments in the area for Sukkot and was providing security.

But the IDF said he and the others involved had acted deceptively and without authorisation.

It said soldiers eventually stopped Sukkot and escorted his group out of Madama after reporting the incident to their commanders.

In a number of previous incidents involving settler violence, soldiers have been filmed standing by without intervening.

The incident has further raised the temperature in the West Bank, where increasing attacks by settlers on Palestinians in recent months have drawn international condemnation.

Madama itself has been the target of several attacks by settlers.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office has issued a statement criticising Sukkot's actions. It read: "Taking the law into one's own hands, especially when it involves public figures, is a reprehensible practice that prevents the IDF from focusing on its missions of combating terrorism and incitement to violence."

Netanyahu's main rival in the upcoming general election, Gadi Eisenkot, said that Sukkot's behaviour was "a disgrace for anyone who claims to represent the public and be a leader".

Eisenkot also criticised Netanyahu for "allowing anarchists like Zvi Sukkot and his ilk to do whatever they please, endangering security in the settlements and harming Israel's standing in the world".

But finance minister Bezalel Smotrich - who heads the Religious Zionism party to which Sukkot belongs - directed his fiercest criticism at what he called the "frantic rush of the left-wing opposition to condemn Sukkot rather than terrorism itself".

On Monday, the most senior Israeli military officer in the West Bank, Major General Avi Bluth, was reported by Israeli media to have told Netanyahu in a closed-door meeting that the mounting violence by settlers could ignite a major escalation.

articles.title: Trump’s Korean gambit exposes a shifting East Asian order
articles.summary: Growing doubts about the US security umbrella are forcing new strategic calculations across the region.
articles.body:
When President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to cut the annual United States-South Korea Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) military exercise planned for mid-August from 11 days to five, he laid bare the transactional logic of his approach to East Asia. The move blindsided Seoul and drew a calculated rebuff from Pyongyang, underscoring how growing doubts about the US defence umbrella are reshaping strategic calculations across the region.

Trump framed the reduction as a goodwill gesture towards Kim Jong Un, whom he described as a leader he “knows very well” and with whom he has a “very good relationship”. He claimed the drills sent a “totally inappropriate and hostile” signal to Pyongyang and linked the decision directly to Seoul’s refusal to join the US war effort in Iran, declaring that America “can’t go around and protect all of these countries, especially when they’re not there to help us”.

Pyongyang’s response to Trump’s overture was carefully calibrated. Kim Yo Jong, Kim Jong Un’s sister, stated she was “unaware” of any communication between the two leaders, contradicting Trump’s claim of a “very positive” exchange. Yet she reaffirmed her brother’s “personally good memories and feelings” towards the US president, signalling that Pyongyang remains open to engagement, but on very different terms: Washington would have to accept North Korea as a nuclear-armed state and abandon what Pyongyang calls its “hostile” policy. Those demands remain fundamentally at odds with Washington’s insistence on complete denuclearisation, raising the prospect that any November meeting could amount to little more than political theatre unless one side changes its position.

China’s response to the renewed prospect of US-North Korea engagement was more restrained, but no less revealing. Beijing was more circumspect about the prospect. Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Lin Jian declined to comment on a possible Trump-Kim meeting. China’s broader position, however, emerged more clearly when Foreign Minister Wang Yi visited Seoul. He urged South Korea to pursue“genuine strategic autonomy” and avoid “bloc confrontation or taking sides”, while calling for accelerated negotiations on the second phase of the China-South Korea Free Trade Agreement and expanded cooperation in AI, the green transition and the digital economy. More significantly, Wang made no reference to denuclearisation and did not endorse Seoul’s multiparty peace initiative, instead speaking of “peaceful coexistence” on the peninsula. The formulation appears to move Beijing closer to accepting the reality of two separate Korean states, rather than continuing to centre denuclearisation as the organising principle of peninsula diplomacy. Notably, Washington appears to be moving in parallel: in the August 25 readout of the Cho Hyun–Marco Rubio call, the US State Department conspicuously omitted any reference to denuclearisation — a term that had appeared routinely in previous trilateral statements as recently as July 22.

Wang also warned against “Japanese right-wing forces’ attempts to reverse the course of history”, urging that “Japanese militarism never be allowed to rise again”. His warning points directly to the speed and scale of Tokyo’s military transformation. Japan under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is moving rapidly to entrench that process. Trump’s latest move did not start this, but it reinforces the logic behind greater Japanese strategic autonomy. On July 31, Tokyo inaugurated its National Intelligence Bureau, strengthening the prime minister’s control over intelligence coordination across government. Japan’s core defence budget has reached a record 9.04 trillion yen ($56.7bn), while Japan says broader defence-related spending has reached its benchmark of 2 percent of gross domestic product ahead of schedule. The buildup is also being embedded in fiscal policy through new defence-related taxes. The pace of this shift has drawn Pyongyang’s wrath: Kim Yo-jong warned Japan that any “wrong choice” would bring “an immediate and unsurvivable, annihilating strike”.

For Beijing, however, the deeper concern is the autonomy of Tokyo’s drive. Japan is seizing the uncertainty surrounding Washington’s commitments to institutionalise military normalisation. Relaxed weapons export rules and deepening symbiosis with defence contractors Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Kawasaki Heavy Industries and IHI, whose combined defence order backlogs reach 6.25 trillion yen ($39.2bn), signal a Japan building the institutional scaffolding for greater independent action. For Beijing, this is the nightmare scenario: A rapidly remilitarised Japan operating not merely as a US proxy, but as an independent great power asserting its own sphere of influence as US credibility frays.

Seoul, too, is recalibrating. On August 18, after Trump ordered the UFS cut, President Lee Jae Myung renewed his push to regain wartime operational control of South Korean forces and accelerate plans for nuclear-powered submarines, arguing that stronger independent defence capabilities should complement the US alliance.

At the centre of this emerging order is a geopolitical triangle: A US treating alliances as transactional commodities, a Japan racing towards permanent military emancipation amid growing uncertainty over US commitments, and a China stabilising its periphery while pushing back against Tokyo’s rightward turn. South Korea, caught in the middle, is increasingly forced to navigate Washington’s unpredictability, Beijing’s economic gravity, and Tokyo’s accelerating militarism.

The uncertainty is profound. If Trump’s rapprochement with Pyongyang produces only theatre, North Korea’s nuclear programme will continue to advance as Beijing and Moscow shield Pyongyang from meaningful external pressure. If Washington’s pressure on Seoul succeeds, South Korea may be dragged deeper into America’s wars, from the Strait of Hormuz to a Taiwan contingency. If Tokyo’s remilitarisation proceeds unchecked, the post-war regional security architecture could be irrevocably altered.

The APEC summit in Shenzhen this November may offer the first real diplomatic test of this emerging order. The prospect of Trump, Xi Jinping, the Japanese and South Korean leaders, and possibly Kim Jong Un converging in one Chinese city would give Beijing an unusually prominent opportunity to shape the diplomatic response to this disorder. Whether it can broker a stabilising understanding, or the summit becomes another stage for competing nationalisms, could help determine East Asia’s trajectory for the decade to come.

The old certainties are eroding. The US alliance system that has anchored the region for three-quarters of a century is being weakened from within. Japan is exploiting the resulting ambiguity to shed post-war constraints. China, preferring a stable periphery and appearing increasingly willing to accommodate a permanent two-state reality on the peninsula, finds itself managing a level of regional uncertainty not seen since the Cold War.

No single summit can arrest the forces driving this transformation. East Asia is entering a new order in which Washington’s ability to set the terms is diminishing, its allies are testing the limits of their dependence, and its rivals are seeking to shape what comes next.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: In 1978, Seoul began dumping its rubbish on a river island; 15 years and 92 million cubic metres of waste later, two 98-metre garbage mountains were sealed beneath five ecological parks
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how Nanjido Island in Seoul transformed from a massive landfill into a beautiful ecological park featuring hiking trails and green spaces, following years of waste disposal and remediation efforts.
articles.body: For fifteen years, a small island on the Han River took in almost everything Seoul threw away. By the time the dumping stopped, the site held two mounds of trash nearly a hundred metres tall. What happened next was a slow process of sealing, planting and rebuilding that transformed one of the cityâs most notorious eyesores into a cluster of public parks with football stadiums, hiking trails and silver grass festivals.1978: Nanjido was chosen after Seoul's existing dump sites reached capacity Waste generation in Seoul in the 1970s was outstripping the capacity of existing waste disposal sites. For instance, areas such as Gunja-dong, Sangwolgok-dong and Yeomchang-dong, which have been dumping grounds since 1964, were becoming overcrowded due to the increased population and construction in Seoul. The government sought a site that would be easily accessible by transportation and chose Nanjido Island in the Han River, where wild orchids used to grow. The research on this history, A Study on the Current Status of Landfill in Seoul and the Solutions to Future Generation Landfill Problems, published in the Journal of Wellbeing Management and Applied Psychology, records that dumping at Nanjido ran from March 1978 to March 1993. During this period, Nanjido served as Seoul's primary waste disposal site, though independent verification of the city's exact population served or the precise share of household waste processed was not available.March 1978 to March 1993: 92 million cubic metres dumped to create two 98 metre high moundsNanjido landfill differed from sanitary landfills of today in not being lined, covered, and controlled in terms of pollution control measures. The study also says Nanjido landfill covered 2,720,000 square metres, roughly the same as Yeouido Island, and that the low-lying fill reached 13 metres above sea level at its highest point in December 1985.Thereafter, the Nanjido landfill site was divided into two parts named Noeul Park and Haneul Park, as documented in Seoul Solutionâs official record of the landfill recovery project. Initially, officials set a 45-metre height limit in line with international standards for sanitary landfill sites. However, due to delays in the construction of the new site at Gimpo, Seoul had to continue filling the site with more waste and ended up with the creation of two high mounds, each of a height of 92 to 98 metres high, storing nearly 92 million cubic metres of waste. Living conditions at the dump were so poor that it was dubbed âSamdado,â or the island of three excesses: dust, smell and flies. Almost 3,000 people collected trash there for a living, recycling paper, bottles and cans, but gas from decomposition caused about 1,390 fires during the dumpâs 15 years of operation.1998 to 2002: Impermeable barriers, leachate treatment and 106 gas wellsSeoul closed Nanjido to new waste in March 1993 and turned its attention to containing the damage already done. The stabilization project formally began in January 1998 and was completed in October 2002, a span of nearly five years. It included impermeable walls to keep leachate from seeping into local groundwater, leachate management, methane gas extraction wells, mound stabilization to reduce the risk of collapse, and a soil cover on both mounds to allow vegetation to grow on top of them. Leachate from the facility had contained a Biological Oxygen Demand of 72 mg/l and a Total Nitrogen concentration of 1,416 mg/l, levels which could contaminate the Han River and its associated groundwaterTo address methane accumulation within the mounds, engineers constructed 106 gas extraction wells distributed evenly across the old landfill at 120-metre intervals. The methane was then used to provide heating for three public sites, including the World Cup Stadium, 40 office buildings, and 16,335 households in surrounding residential areas. The volume of energy extracted from 2002 to 2014 also amounted to almost 43.85 million cubic metres, worth more than 8.7 billion Korean won.Post-capping survey finds exotic species dominating the landfill slopesOnce the mounds were capped, the question became whether anything could grow on ground built entirely from buried rubbish. A vegetation and soil survey, The Plant Community of Nanjido, a Representative Nonsanitary Landfill in South Korea: Implications for Restoration Alternatives, published in Water, Air, & Soil Pollution, set out to answer exactly that. The researchers surveyed the landfill and nearby forest controls with 10 Ã 10 m quadrats, then analysed soil pH, conductivity, organic matter, nutrients, and texture before running canonical correspondence analysis. They found that landfill soils were less acidic and significantly richer in P, Ca and Mg and that the slopes were already dominated by tree species such as Salix babylonica, Robinia pseudoacacia and Ailanthus altissima.Tree species that had taken hold on their own included willow, plane trees, black locust, tree of heaven and Korean forsythia, while Mongolian oak, the region's natural late-successional species, was largely absent from the disturbed ground. The study found that invasive and exotic plants were more common where disturbance was greater, soil conditions differed, and more exotic species were already present. The authors recommended introducing native plant stock from similar disturbed sites and limiting further ground disturbance as the more realistic path toward a stable, native-dominated cover.May 2002: Opening of five parks on the former landfill siteAhead of the Korea-Japan World Cup, the parks opened to the public in May 2002, several months before the broader landfill stabilization project was formally completed in October 2002 The five parks make up World Cup Park, built on the former landfill site and adjacent land. Haneul Park and Noeul Park are located on top of the two old garbage heaps, whereas Pyeonghwa Park and Nanjicheon Park are found on the flattened reclaimed land and Nanji Hangang Park is found along the riverside.The project is widely known internationally. According to Seoul Solution, the city received a Special Award from UN-HABITAT and attracts about 3,000 visitors a year from other countries who come to learn about the project. What began as a last-resort response to a waste problem became a 24-year lesson in restoring heavily polluted land. Methane is still being monitored beneath the turf at Haneul Park, showing that the landfill remains active beneath the surface.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
