articles.title: Massive floods sweep through Nepal; several districts put on high alert
articles.summary: South Asia News: At least eight people were killed and several others are missing after a sudden cloudburst triggered a sharp rise in the Bhotekoshi River, causing wid.
articles.body: At least eight people were killed and several others are missing after a sudden cloudburst triggered a sharp rise in the Bhotekoshi River, causing widespread flooding in Nepalâs Rasuwa district near the China border on Wednesday.Across the border in Tibet, the flooding also reportedly caused âmajor casualtiesâ, according to Chinese state media.The areas of Timure and Syafrubesi were among those badly affected, with vehicles, goods and other property washed away.âA sudden flood in Rasuwa has caused damage to the market area, including Syaprubesi. Initial reports have come that the flood that has been occurring for some time has caused great damage to the settlement and market area. The exact details of the flood damage have not yet been received,â said Narendra Pariyar, chief district officer of Rasuwa.The floodwater reportedly came from the direction of Tibet and surged through the Bhote Koshi River around 9 am local time.The Nepal army said the sudden rise in water caused widespread destruction in Timure and the nearby Syafrubesi area. Vehicles, goods and other property were swept away.Rasuwa district is located northeast of Kathmandu, around 125 km from the Tibet border.High alert in several districtsThe National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRM) has asked people living near river banks in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan and Gorkha to remain on high alert and take necessary safety measures until further notice.Rasuwa assistant chief district officer Dhruva Prasad Adhikari said the scale of the flooding was unusually large and that the two settlements had suffered significant damage.Rasuwa chief customs officer Rajendra Dhungana said several vehicles and goods kept at the customs premises were swept away. A recently constructed bridge was also destroyed.Rescue operations under wayThe Nepal Prime Ministerâs Office said personnel from the Nepal army, armed police force and Nepal Police had been deployed in Rasuwa and nearby areas to strengthen rescue and relief operations.A high-level meeting will also be held to assess the situation and decide on further measures, according to the PMâs Office.The Nepal army has sent two helicopters to areas near the Trishuli River for search and rescue operations. An MI-17 helicopter equipped with an Emergency Medical Rescue Team has also been sent towards the district hospital in Trishuli, the army said.The army said details of the damage were still being collected and the full extent of the destruction was not yet known.Not caused by rainfallAccording to Nepalâs department of hydrology and meteorology, Wednesdayâs flooding was not caused by rainfall in Rasuwa.The development comes a year after two catastrophic floods hit the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa, killing at least 10 people.That flooding was caused by the sudden draining of a previously unnoticed âsupraglacialâ lake.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Savannah audited 39,000 Flock searches and found 34 unjustified; 6 employees were fired and 4 have now been arrested
articles.summary: US News: Four former Savannah Police Department employees were arrested on Friday after an investigation into the alleged misuse of the Flock Safety license pl.
articles.body: Four former Savannah Police Department employees were arrested on Friday after an investigation into the alleged misuse of the Flock Safety license plate reader system.The former employees have been booked into the Chatham County Jail, local broadcaster WTOC reported. Out of them, three are former police officers, while the fourth worked as a community service specialist. All four had been fired from the Savannah Police Department earlier in August.It all started with internal investigation by the Savannah Police Department on July 27. Two days later, the department asked the Georgia Bureau of Investigation (GBI) to look into the case.The internal audit examined 39,000 Flock searches made so far this year. Of those, 127 searches were flagged for review. The police department determined that 34 of the searches were unjustified. Six employees were ultimately fired, although only four have been arrested so far.Flock searches on family, acquaintances The four arrested employees are 48-year-old Marquis Dillard, 23-year-old Donald Phillips, 39-year-old Matthew Rich and 34-year-old Calandic Thomas.Dillard, Phillips and Rich are former officers. Each faces two counts of misuse of a license plate reader system and two counts of violation of oath of office. Thomas, a former community service specialist, faces two counts of misuse of a license plate reader system.According to the City of Savannah, Dillard spent 10 years with the Savannah Police Department and most recently worked as a homicide detective before his termination. Phillips had worked for the department for two-and-a-half years. Rich served with the department for 13 years before he was fired. Thomas worked as a community service specialist for just under three years.The four former employees are accused of running Flock license plate searches on personal acquaintances and family members. One of the officers is also accused of giving an outside agency unauthorised access to the system.The GBI confirmed that the outside agency is also part of its investigation. However, it has not identified the agency.Flock license plate reader systems allow law enforcement agencies to search information collected by cameras. Savannah has 106 Flock cameras, and Georgia has the second-most Flock cameras of any state in the US.'Breach of public trust'Savannah Mayor Van Johnson criticised the alleged misuse of the technology and the breach of public trust.âWe entrusted these individuals with advanced technology, and even more importantly, with the publicâs trust,â Johnson said. âNobody is above the law, and everyone trusted with public confidence is accountable,â he added, as quoted by WTOC.Police Chief Lenny Gunther also said department employees must follow the law and maintain professional standards.âThe actions of a few do not reflect the dedication and professionalism of the men and women who honorably serve our community every day,â Gunther said.Gunther said he is working to introduce a formal policy governing the use of Flock cameras. The department also plans to conduct weekly inspections using its audit-assist tool to identify possible misuse earlier.Flock technology faces scrutinyThe Savannah case has added to wider concerns about how automated license plate reader systems are used and monitored.Police departments say the technology can help investigators locate missing people, recover stolen vehicles and investigate serious crimes. However, the systems have also raised questions about privacy, data access and how information collected by the cameras is shared.CBS News reported that the Savannah arrests are part of a growing list of alleged misuse cases involving automated license plate readers in Georgia. In July, five former Albany police officers were arrested after an internal audit found they had accessed retained Flock license plate data for non-law-enforcement purposes.Georgia already has rules governing license plate data held by law enforcement agencies. Under state law, such data can be accessed only for a law enforcement purpose. Agencies can share the information with other law enforcement agencies for those purposes.The law also requires agencies using automated license plate recognition systems to maintain policies governing their use and officer training. Knowingly obtaining or using the data under false pretences or for another purpose can result in a misdemeanor of a high and aggravated nature.Flock Safety has also announced changes to its safeguards. CEO Garrett Langley said the company is moving towards a seven-day default retention period for license plate reader data, down from 30 days. Evidence connected to active investigations can still be preserved.The company also says law enforcement customers will be required to use its Audit Assistance system, which is designed to flag unusual search activity. Other changes include requiring case codes for searches and automatically suspending access in some situations until suspicious activity can be reviewed. âWe're setting a higher bar for ourselves and the industry,â Langley said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Hawaii mixed recycled fishing nets into an Oahu road; 11 months later, researchers found no more polyethylene microplastics than in regular asphalt
articles.summary: US News: Hawaii is addressing its plastic waste crisis by melting recycled fishing gear into asphalt, revealing insights on microplastics in roads after an 11-month test.
articles.body: Shipping waste off HawaiÊ»i's islands is expensive, local landfills are running out of room, and Pacific currents keep depositing tons of derelict fishing gear onto the shoreline. Researchers at HawaiÊ»i Pacific University tested whether washed-up plastic could be melted into asphalt and returned about 11 months later to test whether the road was shedding microplastics back into the environment.Derelict fishing gear becomes HawaiÊ»i's largest marine debris problemJennifer Lynch, director of CMDR at HawaiÊ»i Pacific University, says most debris in Hawaiian waters consists of fishing nets and fishing lines that drift in from elsewhere. HawaiÊ»i has been adopting polymer-modified asphalt since around 2020 for its improved resistance to cracking, rutting and water damage in the state's tropical climate. That pavement is normally made by melting a virgin plastic copolymer into the asphalt binder before it is mixed with heated rock and sand.However, the HawaiÊ»i Department of Transportation wondered if some of that virgin plastic could be replaced by recycled plastic, such as the abandoned fishing equipment that was being washed ashore on the beaches of the island state. The agency asked Lynch's group to supply fishing nets for the asphalt mix and to determine whether the asphalt would shed more microplastics than regular asphalt.CMDR's Bounty Project removes tons of fishing gear from the Pacific CMDR has implemented an initiative known as the Bounty Program, whereby commercial licensed fishermen are rewarded for retrieving lost fishing equipment, according to HawaiÊ»i Pacific Universityâs announcement of the project. As of the study's presentation in March 2026, HawaiÊ»i Pacific University reported the initiative had retrieved 84 tons of large fishing equipment from the Pacific. Science News separately reported a running total closer to 90 metric tons of plastic trash pulled from the ocean by that point, a discrepancy the two sources do not reconcile, and which may reflect a difference between short tons and metric tons rather than a factual error.After the nets and plastic collected through the Bounty Program were processed for use in asphalt, the HawaiÊ»i Department of Transportation moved the experimental mixtures onto a real road. The local construction firm poured pavement of a residential road on the island of Oahu using various mixtures of asphalt: the control sample using regular copolymer, a mixture using recycled polyethylene gathered from recycling bins in Honolulu and a mixture using recycled polyethylene from fishing nets.Researchers return after 11 months to sample road dust for microplastics Instead of testing the pavement in the laboratory and calling it done, Lynchâs group let the road lie under normal traffic first. Around 11 months into the study, the researchers routinely swept up the road dust found in segments of asphalt pavement to see if the wear and tear had released microplastics into the dirt. In the laboratory, the dust was processed to extract different types of polymer material, including microplastics, larger plastic fragments and tire-wear rubber.The team was able to infer which source the polymers came from using pyrolysis gas chromatography mass spectrometry. The researchers traced styrene and butadiene to the standard pavement, polyethylene to the plastic-waste and fishing-net mixes, and isoprene and butadiene rubber to tire wear.Tire wear swamps the polyethylene signal in the test results The recycled polyethylene pavement did not lose more plastic than the control pavement in lab wear tests or in stormwater runoff samples. In the dust, microplastic-sized particles appeared no matter which pavement mix was tested, but very few of those particles were identified as polyethylene. The recycled plastic is melted directly into the asphalt binder, which means that anything that ultimately breaks loose can be a fused mass of rock, binder and polymer, rather than loose plastic. Lynch says itâs a difference from other additive technologies.The researchers initially had difficulty isolating the companion signal from the tire-wear noise. According to Lynch, the readings showed huge peaks, indicating that tire wear overwhelmed the polyethylene signal by orders of magnitude. The team had to pick through the chromatogram readings to see if they could find any signal from the recycled plastic at all.According to the American Chemical Society's press release on the study, more work is needed on longâterm durability. Researchers say conclusions do not answer every question about how the pavement holds up over years of use. But for a state running out of places to put its plastic waste, an 11-month road test that sheds no more microplastic than ordinary asphalt is a promising start.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1998, Israel closed the Hiriya landfill after decades of waste had formed a 60-metre mound; years later, methane wells, trees and trails helped transform the site into the centrepiece of a 2,000-acre park
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how the former Hiriya landfill in Israel evolved into the lush Ariel Sharon Park, a prime example of urban reclamation and sustainable design, transforming environmental hazards into a thriving green space.
articles.body: In August 1998, Israel closed the Hiriya landfill after almost five decades of receiving waste from the Dan Region. By then, the site had grown into a garbage hill of roughly 60 metres high. This huge landfill footprint accounted for an estimated 25 million tons of accumulated waste, a figure supported by a 2006 peer-reviewed study that calculated the physical volume of the buried material at approximately 16 million cubic metres. The landfillâs closure, however, did not remove the mountain; instead, it began a long process of engineering, gas management and landscape rehabilitation that eventually led to the former dump becoming the centrepiece of Ariel Sharon Park, a planned metropolitan park covering about 2,000 acres.An accumulating waste mountain turns into an environmental hazardHiriya opened in 1952 and became the principal waste-disposal ground for most of the Dan Region. According to O. Ayalon, N. Becker and E. Shaniâs 2006 study published in Waste Management, the landfill operated until 1998 and developed into a major environmental hazard. When the site closed, approximately 16 million cubic metres of waste were estimated to remain buried there. The study also identified several problems requiring rehabilitation, including greenhouse gas emissions, unstable slopes and leachate formation.The moundâs location made things even more complicated, with the landfillâs proximity to Ben Gurion Airport and the birds attracted by decomposing waste. Contemporary accounts identified those birds as an aviation hazard because of their proximity to aircraft during takeoff and landing. However, the bird problem was only one part of a larger environmental challenge that included leachate, landfill gas, instability and the sheer scale of the waste mound.The 2006 study pointed out that closing the landfill did not mean simply walking away from it. While emergency interim measures were deployed immediately in 1998 to manage urgent bird hazards and slope stability, comprehensive, long-term rehabilitation efforts began in 2001, including site investigations, engineering and scientific evaluations and planning for the landscapeâs eventual use. The conclusion notes that engineering rehabilitation was necessary to make a public park possible, while converting the site into a park provided the strongest justification for the wider reclamation attempt.Methane wells help stabilise the waste mountainOne of the most persistent problems faced by the authorities was the landfill gas. Organic material buried in the mountain continued to decompose after the landfill stopped accepting waste, producing methane.
